            - generic [ref=e93]:
              - generic [ref=e94]:
                - heading "Abstract" [level=2] [ref=e95]: Abstract
                - paragraph [ref=e96]:
                  - text: Systems metabolic engineering, which recently emerged as metabolic engineering integrated with systems biology, synthetic biology, and evolutionary engineering, allows engineering of microorganisms on a systemic level for the production of valuable chemicals far beyond its native capabilities. Here, we review the strategies for systems metabolic engineering and particularly its applications in
                  - emphasis [ref=e97]: Escherichia coli
                  - text: . First, we cover the various tools developed for genetic manipulation in
                  - emphasis [ref=e98]: E. coli
                  - text: to increase the production titers of desired chemicals. Next, we detail the strategies for systems metabolic engineering in
                  - emphasis [ref=e99]: E. coli
                  - text: ", covering the engineering of the native metabolism, the expansion of metabolism with synthetic pathways, and the process engineering aspects undertaken to achieve higher production titers of desired chemicals. Finally, we examine a couple of notable products as case studies produced in"
                  - emphasis [ref=e100]: E. coli
                  - text: strains developed by systems metabolic engineering. The large portfolio of chemical products successfully produced by engineered
                  - emphasis [ref=e101]: E. coli
                  - text: listed here demonstrates the sheer capacity of what can be envisioned and achieved with respect to microbial production of chemicals. Systems metabolic engineering is no longer in its infancy; it is now widely employed and is also positioned to further embrace next-generation interdisciplinary principles and innovation for its upgrade. Systems metabolic engineering will play increasingly important roles in developing industrial strains including
                  - emphasis [ref=e102]: E. coli
                  - text: that are capable of efficiently producing natural and nonnatural chemicals and materials from renewable nonfood biomass.
              - generic [ref=e103]:
                - heading "INTRODUCTION" [level=2] [ref=e104]: INTRODUCTION
                - paragraph [ref=e105]:
                  - emphasis [ref=e106]: Escherichia coli
                  - text: has become not only one of the most characterized and understood organisms, but also the most sought organism for genetic manipulation since the success of the first ever genetically modified
                  - emphasis [ref=e107]: E. coli
                  - text: in 1973 that pioneered the field of genetic engineering (
                  - link "1" [ref=e108] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b1"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "2" [ref=e109] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b2"
                  - text: ). As a Gram-negative facultative anaerobe,
                  - emphasis [ref=e110]: E. coli
                  - text: is one of the first colonizers in neonatal intestines and normally dwells in gastrointestinal microflora of many animals, including humans (
                  - link "3" [ref=e111] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b3"
                  - text: ). Although these enteric bacteria might develop virulence through horizontal gene transfer (
                  - link "4" [ref=e112] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b4"
                  - text: ), genetic manipulation in laboratory settings is simple and quick, rendering the strain attractive for research. Following the initial sequencing of the genome with 4.6 Mb size and about 4,300 genes annotated (
                  - link "5" [ref=e113] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b5"
                  - text: ), the pangenome with a reservoir of almost 13,000 genes has been recently characterized (
                  - link "6" [ref=e114] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b6"
                  - text: ). With the genome sequence readily available, the massive influx of omics information and the development of various engineering tools enabled our attempts to understand
                  - emphasis [ref=e115]: E. coli
                  - text: at the systems level.
                - paragraph [ref=e116]:
                  - text: Systems metabolic engineering emerged as the fields of metabolic engineering and biotechnology transitioned toward understanding the biology of organisms at the systems level. In 1991, metabolic engineering was first described and aimed to be a field concerning the application of recombinant DNA methods to develop high-performance strains for the production of useful chemicals and recombinant proteins (
                  - link "7" [ref=e117] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b7"
                  - text: ). In the same year, the historical issuance of U.S. patent 5,000,000 appeared, granting rights to converting hexose or pentose to ethanol with a genetically modified
                  - emphasis [ref=e118]: E. coli
                  - text: expressing
                  - emphasis [ref=e119]: Zymomonas mobilis
                  - text: pyruvate decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase (
                  - link "8" [ref=e120] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b8"
                  - text: ). Together with the ever-growing omics data, rapidly advancing tools, and novel strategies, it is now possible to rationally design high-performance
                  - emphasis [ref=e121]: E. coli
                  - text: strains for producing not only ethanol but also higher alcohols (
                  - link "9" [ref=e122] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b9"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "10" [ref=e123] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b10"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "11" [ref=e124] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b11"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "12" [ref=e125] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b12"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "13" [ref=e126] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b13"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "14" [ref=e127] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b14"
                  - text: ), hydrocarbons (
                  - link "15" [ref=e128] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b15"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "16" [ref=e129] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b16"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "17" [ref=e130] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b17"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "18" [ref=e131] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b18"
                  - text: ), amino acids (
                  - link "19" [ref=e132] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b19"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "20" [ref=e133] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b20"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "21" [ref=e134] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b21"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "22" [ref=e135] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b22"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "23" [ref=e136] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b23"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "24" [ref=e137] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b24"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "25" [ref=e138] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b25"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "26" [ref=e139] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b26"
                  - text: ), various polymer precursors (
                  - link "27" [ref=e140] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b27"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "28" [ref=e141] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b28"
                  - text: ), recombinant proteins (
                  - link "29" [ref=e142] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b29"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "30" [ref=e143] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b30"
                  - text: ), and plastics (
                  - link "31" [ref=e144] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b31"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "32" [ref=e145] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b32"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "33" [ref=e146] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b33"
                  - text: ). Some of these production processes have achieved industrial-level production standards (greater than 100 g/liter production titer and 3 to 4 g/L/h productivity) and have been commercialized to meet the global market demands.
                - paragraph [ref=e147]:
                  - text: Systems metabolic engineering continues to expand at an unparalleled pace with the rapid development of state-of-the-art genetic manipulation strategies, high-throughput screening tools, computational analysis methods, cultivation strategies, and downstream processes (
                  - link "Fig. 1" [ref=e148] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#fig1"
                  - text: ). In this contribution, we aim to outline both the traditional and the most recently developed genetic manipulation tools including zinc finger nucleases (ZFN), transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALEN), multiplex automated genome engineering (MAGE), conjugative assembly genome engineering (CAGE), clustered regularly interspaced palindromic repeat (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) systems, and global transcription machinery engineering (gTME), in light of systems metabolic engineering. We also cover strategies for systems metabolic engineering and approaches to arising issues including enhancement of biosynthetic pathway, improving carbon flux, creating novel pathways, transporter engineering, reducing acetic acid formation during high-cell-density cultivation (HCDC), and the use of plasmids without antibiotics. Additionally, the concerted application of these strategies for industrial-level production of chemical production is detailed. While we confine our discussion to focus on the systems metabolic engineering of
                  - emphasis [ref=e149]: E. coli
                  - text: ", readers are encouraged to explore various publications on the successful applications of the strategies developed for other species as well ("
                  - link "34" [ref=e150] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b34"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "35" [ref=e151] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b35"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "36" [ref=e152] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b36"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "37" [ref=e153] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b37"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "38" [ref=e154] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b38"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "39" [ref=e155] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b39"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "40" [ref=e156] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b40"
                  - text: ","
                  - link "41" [ref=e157] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#b41"
                  - text: ).
                - figure "Overview of systems metabolic engineering. Systems metabolic engineering is the recursive process of improving a candidate strain via pathway engineering, transporter engineering, omics tools, and in silico analysis in an effort to increase the production of desired chemicals to industrial scales." [ref=e158]:
                  - heading "Figure 1." [level=3] [ref=e159]
                  - paragraph [ref=e160]:
                    - img "Figure 1" [ref=e161]
                  - link "Open in a new tab" [ref=e163] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: figure/fig1/
                  - paragraph [ref=e165]:
                    - strong [ref=e166]: Overview of systems metabolic engineering.
                    - text: Systems metabolic engineering is the recursive process of improving a candidate strain via pathway engineering, transporter engineering, omics tools, and
                    - emphasis [ref=e167]: in silico
                    - text: analysis in an effort to increase the production of desired chemicals to industrial scales.
              - generic [ref=e168]:
                - heading "TOOLS FOR SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF E. COLI" [level=2] [ref=e169]:
                  - text: TOOLS FOR SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF
                  - emphasis [ref=e170]: E. COLI
                - paragraph [ref=e171]:
                  - text: Here, we cover the various tools developed for genetic and genomic manipulations in
                  - emphasis [ref=e172]: E. coli
                  - text: . Some of these tools were not initially developed specifically for the purposes of systems metabolic engineering, but we listed them nonetheless, because these tools have become an integral part of strain development and, thus, a part of systems metabolic engineering. It must also be noted that some of these tools are very specific to
                  - emphasis [ref=e173]: E. coli
                  - text: ", and applications of such tools on other organisms might not have been studied."
                - generic [ref=e174]:
                  - 'heading "Recombineering: Recombination-Mediated Genetic Engineering" [level=3] [ref=e175]'
                  - paragraph [ref=e176]:
                    - text: While the traditional cloning methodology, comprising digesting vectors with restriction enzymes and subsequent joining of the ends by ligation
                    - emphasis [ref=e177]: in vitro
                    - text: ", is the starting point for almost all molecular biology experiments, it is not suitable for complex procedures (e.g., large-sized DNA manipulation). In recombination-mediated genetic engineering or “recombineering,” components derived from phages, λ and P1, have not only been the center of focus but also the most commonly used tools. Recombineering method has been used for engineering plasmids ("
                    - link "42" [ref=e178] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b42"
                    - text: ), genomic DNAs, and bacterial artificial chromosomes (BACs) (
                    - link "43" [ref=e179] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b43"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "44" [ref=e180] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b44"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "45" [ref=e181] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b45"
                    - text: ), effectively using either single-stranded DNA (ssDNA)- (
                    - link "46" [ref=e182] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b46"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "47" [ref=e183] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b47"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "48" [ref=e184] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b48"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "49" [ref=e185] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b49"
                    - text: ) or double-stranded DNA (dsDNA)-based techniques (
                    - link "50" [ref=e186] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b50"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "51" [ref=e187] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b51"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "52" [ref=e188] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b52"
                    - text: ). In a metabolic engineering context, this process is used to alter expression levels of native proteins for flux optimization (
                    - link "53" [ref=e189] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b53"
                    - text: ). In general, such methods rely on
                    - emphasis [ref=e190]: E. coli
                    - text: native recombination machinery originally used in DNA repair mechanisms.
                  - paragraph [ref=e191]:
                    - text: The homologous recombination mechanism of
                    - emphasis [ref=e192]: E. coli
                    - text: that has most commonly been utilized in recombineering is the
                    - emphasis [ref=e193]: recABCD
                    - text: pathway. RecA is involved not only in homologous recombination but also in DNA repair and exhibits multiple functions, including DNA binding, ATP binding, DNA hydrolysis, protein degradation, and filament formation (
                    - link "54" [ref=e194] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b54"
                    - text: ). RecBCD, also known as ExoV, exhibits helicase and exonuclease activities (
                    - link "55" [ref=e195] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b55"
                    - text: ) and facilitates initial steps in DNA repair mechanism (for RecBCD reviews, see references
                    - link "56" [ref=e196] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b56"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "57" [ref=e197] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b57"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "58" [ref=e198] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b58"
                    - text: ). In
                    - emphasis [ref=e199]: E. coli
                    - text: ", RecBCD degrades along linear DNA until it encounters a"
                    - emphasis [ref=e200]: cis
                    - text: "-element,"
                    - emphasis [ref=e201]: chi
                    - text: (crossover hotspot instigator or
                    - emphasis [ref=e202]: χ
                    - text: ) sequence, which facilitates the subsequent steps in recombination events (
                    - link "57" [ref=e203] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b57"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "59" [ref=e204] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b59"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "60" [ref=e205] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b60"
                    - text: ). Linear dsDNA-based recombineering had been discouraged in the past, in particular because of
                    - emphasis [ref=e206]: E. coli
                    - text: RecBCD mechanisms, although linear dsDNA transformation in yeast had been common (
                    - link "61" [ref=e207] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b61"
                    - text: ). While successful transformation with linear dsDNA in the
                    - emphasis [ref=e208]: recBC
                    - text: disrupted strain marks one of the first recombineering cases in historical perspective (
                    - link "62" [ref=e209] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b62"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "63" [ref=e210] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b63"
                    - text: ), it required additional disruption of
                    - emphasis [ref=e211]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. sbcB" [ref=e212] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10926
                    - text: and
                    - emphasis [ref=e213]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. sbcC" [ref=e214] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10927
                    - text: because they often impede the use of linear dsDNA for homologous recombination template in the absence of functional RecBCD (
                    - link "62" [ref=e215] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b62"
                    - text: ). While the strict requirement for
                    - emphasis [ref=e216]: recBC
                    - text: deficiency for linearized dsDNA transformation can be evaded by flanking linear dsDNA with the
                    - emphasis [ref=e217]: chi
                    - text: sequence, the
                    - emphasis [ref=e218]: chi
                    - text: "-mediated recombineering suffers from low efficiency and positive-negative selection requirement ("
                    - link "64" [ref=e219] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b64"
                    - text: ). Use of λ recombination system for exonuclease deficiency requirement is one way to avoid this issue.
                  - paragraph [ref=e220]:
                    - text: The λ recombination system designated “Red” consists of two proteins, the exonuclease (simply
                    - link "External, opens in a new tab. exo" [ref=e221] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG12372
                    - text: or sometimes α) and the bet protein (simply β) (
                    - link "65" [ref=e222] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b65"
                    - text: ). Red is assisted by a third λ protein, gam (or γ), which increases
                    - link "External, opens in a new tab. exo" [ref=e223] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG12372
                    - text: and β activity on linear dsDNA by inhibiting
                    - emphasis [ref=e224]: E. coli
                    - text: RecBCD exonucleases (
                    - link "50" [ref=e225] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b50"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "55" [ref=e226] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b55"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "66" [ref=e227] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b66"
                    - text: ). Since the presence of RecBCD no longer hinders stability of dsDNA, Red is universally applicable and greatly improves the linear dsDNA transformation efficiency as well as recombination (
                    - link "50" [ref=e228] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b50"
                    - text: ). This system is often used in conjunction with site-specific recombination systems such as Cre/
                    - emphasis [ref=e229]: lox
                    - text: and Flp/
                    - emphasis [ref=e230]: FRT
                    - text: system.
                  - paragraph [ref=e231]:
                    - text: Initially discovered in early 1980s, the Cre/
                    - emphasis [ref=e232]: lox
                    - text: system exploits the phage P1 infection mechanism in
                    - emphasis [ref=e233]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "67" [ref=e234] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b67"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "68" [ref=e235] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b68"
                    - text: ). As a member of the λ recombinase family with a relatively small size (38 kDa), Cre (short for cause of recombination) protein from P1 recognizes and integrates the
                    - emphasis [ref=e236]: lox
                    - text: P (short for locus of crossover (x) in P1) sequence into a specific location of bacterial chromosome (
                    - emphasis [ref=e237]: lox
                    - text: B) in a Holliday junction-mediated event. Initially discovered from yeast plasmid “2μ circle” (
                    - link "69" [ref=e238] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b69"
                    - text: ), the Flp/
                    - emphasis [ref=e239]: FRT
                    - text: (Flp recognition target) system is analogous to Cre/
                    - emphasis [ref=e240]: lox
                    - text: and uses two inverted repeats (
                    - link "70" [ref=e241] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b70"
                    - text: ). While recognition sites in both systems are 34 base pairs (bp), Cre is more thermostable than Flp (
                    - link "71" [ref=e242] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b71"
                    - text: ) and exhibits higher DNA binding affinity cooperativity (
                    - link "72" [ref=e243] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b72"
                    - text: ). For engineering multiple genes, mutant
                    - emphasis [ref=e244]: lox
                    - text: sequences such as
                    - emphasis [ref=e245]: lox
                    - text: 71,
                    - emphasis [ref=e246]: lox
                    - text: 66, and
                    - emphasis [ref=e247]: lox
                    - text: 2272 are also available for preventing further recombination events (
                    - link "73" [ref=e248] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b73"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "74" [ref=e249] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b74"
                    - text: ). In conjunction with such site-specific recombination mechanisms in the above-mentioned homologous recombination, more efficient genetic engineering methods are being continuously developed.
                  - paragraph [ref=e250]:
                    - text: The λ Red system combined with site-specific recombination was successful by the establishment of a one-step inactivation method for chromosomal deletion of
                    - emphasis [ref=e251]: E. coli
                    - text: genes (
                    - link "52" [ref=e252] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b52"
                    - text: ). Widely accepted and used in systems metabolic engineering, this method employs the PCR-generated linear DNA including a drug selectable marker and homology extensions at both ends for recombination that are additionally flanked by
                    - emphasis [ref=e253]: lox
                    - text: (or
                    - emphasis [ref=e254]: FRT
                    - text: ). Plasmid-based introduction of λ Red genes allows linear dsDNA integration into genome (
                    - link "52" [ref=e255] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b52"
                    - text: ) followed by site-specific recombination for “pop out” of the selectable marker, successfully deleting the target gene (
                    - link "75" [ref=e256] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b75"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "76" [ref=e257] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b76"
                    - text: ). Time taken for engineering of multiple genes has been improved recently using an integrated system for both recombination mechanisms (
                    - link "77" [ref=e258] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b77"
                    - text: ). Because the two recombination systems were both integrated into one helper plasmid, there is no need for plasmid curing or repeated transformation for sequential genome-editing steps, thus greatly reducing the time taken for sequential recombinations (
                    - link "77" [ref=e259] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b77"
                    - text: "). While this method boasts seamless efficiency and speed, the system leaves a scar in the edited genome. One way to overcome this challenge is to use a dual-selection system for the removal of the selection marker: a widely used dual-selection system involves the use of a gene named"
                    - emphasis [ref=e260]: sacB
                    - text: .
                  - paragraph [ref=e261]:
                    - text: Isolated from
                    - emphasis [ref=e262]: Bacillus subtilis
                    - text: ", the"
                    - emphasis [ref=e263]: sacB
                    - text: gene encoding levansucrase is used as a negative selection marker for an insertion sequence (
                    - link "78" [ref=e264] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b78"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "79" [ref=e265] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b79"
                    - text: ). The
                    - emphasis [ref=e266]: sacB
                    - text: gene is usually used in conjunction with an antibiotic resistance gene for a two-step selection process to validate a homologous recombination of the host genomic DNA with the sequence of interest (
                    - link "80" [ref=e267] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b80"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "81" [ref=e268] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b81"
                    - text: ). A plasmid harboring antibiotic resistance,
                    - emphasis [ref=e269]: sacB
                    - text: ", and engineered sequence is introduced into a host cell, where the first level of screening is done on a medium plate containing the respective antibiotic to ensure proper genome integration of the plasmid. Once transformation of the plasmid is confirmed, the consequent host cells are then introduced into a sucrose-rich medium for a second level of screening; levansucrase converts sucrose into lethal levan. Only the host cells with successful second recombination will survive, thus validating the change in the genomic DNA of the host; some population with the second cross-over occurring at the same side as the first cross-over will revert to their original state and fail to survive. Survival of cells with spontaneous mutation in"
                    - emphasis [ref=e270]: sacB
                    - text: coding region is the weakness of this system.
                - generic [ref=e271]:
                  - heading "Meganucleases" [level=3] [ref=e272]
                  - paragraph [ref=e273]:
                    - text: "Meganucleases, also known as homing endonucleases, are deoxyribonucleases that cleave recognition sites that are 12 to 40 bp long. Based on sequences and structural motifs, they are categorized into five classes: LAGLIDADG, GIY-YIG, HNH, His-Cys box, and PD-(D/E)XK; LAGLIDADG especially is the largest family that is found in all kingdoms of life ("
                    - link "82" [ref=e274] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b82"
                    - text: "). Meganucleases are easily distinguished from other restriction enzymes by special prefixes in their names: I- for those found in introns ("
                    - link "83" [ref=e275] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b83"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "84" [ref=e276] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b84"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "85" [ref=e277] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b85"
                    - text: ), PI- for those found in inteins (protein inserts) (
                    - link "86" [ref=e278] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b86"
                    - text: ), F- for viral genes and those freestanding outside introns and inteins (
                    - link "87" [ref=e279] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b87"
                    - text: ), and E- or H- for engineered or hybrid meganucleases (
                    - link "88" [ref=e280] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b88"
                    - text: ). The first meganuclease identified is I-
                    - emphasis [ref=e281]: Sce
                    - text: I, found in the mitochondria of baker’s yeast
                    - emphasis [ref=e282]: Saccharomyces cerevisiae
                    - text: (
                    - link "89" [ref=e283] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b89"
                    - text: ). Subsequently, several other meganucleases, including I-
                    - emphasis [ref=e284]: Cre
                    - text: I from the chloroplasts of a green alga
                    - emphasis [ref=e285]: Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
                    - text: (
                    - link "84" [ref=e286] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b84"
                    - text: ) and I-
                    - emphasis [ref=e287]: Dmo
                    - text: I from an archaeon
                    - emphasis [ref=e288]: Desulfurococcus mobilis
                    - text: (
                    - link "85" [ref=e289] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b85"
                    - text: ), were identified and characterized.
                  - paragraph [ref=e290]:
                    - text: The relatively long nature of meganuclease recognition sites explains their extremely low appearance frequency, which has inspired scientists to use them as a site-specific genome engineering or gene therapy tool. Mathematically, one recognition site 40 bp in length would only appear once in 1.2 × 10
                    - superscript [ref=e291]: "24"
                    - text: bp. In reality, one or more recognition sites occur in each genome of certain organisms. However, the scarcity of recognition sites in genomes also makes the use of meganucleases for direct engineering difficult because of the lack of variety and options for suitable use in a given genomic locus of interest. Two approaches have been taken to overcome this obstacle. In one approach, target DNA specificities were altered by either creating mutant meganucleases (
                    - link "90" [ref=e292] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b90"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "91" [ref=e293] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b91"
                    - text: ) or chimeras using different parental nucleases (
                    - link "88" [ref=e294] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b88"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "92" [ref=e295] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b92"
                    - text: ). In another approach, a meganuclease recognition sequence is inserted into the genomic locus of interest (
                    - link "89" [ref=e296] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b89"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "93" [ref=e297] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b93"
                    - text: ). In either case, DNA cleavage followed by homologous recombinations at the target loci can be induced for desired chromosomal engineering (
                    - link "89" [ref=e298] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b89"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "92" [ref=e299] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b92"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "93" [ref=e300] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b93"
                    - text: ). Alternatively, the scarcity of recognition sites in the genome that may pose a problem can be circumvented with the following novel strategy. When the organism of interest lacks the recognition sequence in the genome, the sequence can be introduced on a plasmid for
                    - emphasis [ref=e301]: in vivo
                    - text: cleavage, leading either to the loss of plasmids (
                    - link "94" [ref=e302] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b94"
                    - text: ) or integrations of the linearized plasmids into the genome (
                    - link "94" [ref=e303] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b94"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "95" [ref=e304] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b95"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e305]:
                  - heading "Zinc Finger Nucleases (ZFNs)" [level=3] [ref=e306]
                  - paragraph [ref=e307]:
                    - text: As described in “Meganucleases” above, finding or synthesizing endonucleases that target and cleave desired sequences in a very specific manner has been a big concern in the field of genome engineering. Often described as “programmable nucleases,” such endonucleases have been designed and manufactured since the first report on the creation of a fusion endonuclease, named “zinc finger nucleases” (ZFNs) (
                    - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e308] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig2"
                    - text: ). In a 1996 study, zinc finger domains were combined with fragments of a restriction endonuclease, producing the first ZFN (
                    - link "96" [ref=e309] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b96"
                    - text: ). In this first article on ZFN, the authors employed zinc finger proteins CP-QDR and Sp1-QNR, which consist of three domains of Cys
                    - subscript [ref=e310]: "2"
                    - text: His
                    - subscript [ref=e311]: "2"
                    - text: zinc fingers and thus bind to 9-bp target sequences (
                    - link "96" [ref=e312] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b96"
                    - text: ). Moreover, removing the N terminus of FokI restriction endonuclease, which is responsible for the DNA binding activity (
                    - link "97" [ref=e313] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b97"
                    - text: ), C-terminal 196 amino acids of
                    - emphasis [ref=e314]: Fok
                    - text: I, which has the nonspecific DNA cleavage activity (
                    - link "98" [ref=e315] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b98"
                    - text: ), was fused to the C terminus of each zinc finger protein (
                    - link "96" [ref=e316] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b96"
                    - text: ). Maximally utilizing the requirement of
                    - emphasis [ref=e317]: Fok
                    - text: I dimerization to work as a DNA cleaving unit (
                    - link "99" [ref=e318] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b99"
                    - text: ), a genomic locus of interest can be more specifically targeted by using two ZFNs, which bind to both of the flanking regions of the target site separated 5 to 7 bp apart from each other. The homodimerization of the wild-type
                    - emphasis [ref=e319]: Fok
                    - text: I domains, however, results in off-target cleavage issues, and this was solved by generating obligate heterodimeric
                    - emphasis [ref=e320]: Fok
                    - text: I C-terminal domains by the modification of their dimerization interfaces (
                    - link "100" [ref=e321] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b100"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "101" [ref=e322] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b101"
                    - text: ). Moreover, enhancement of the
                    - emphasis [ref=e323]: Fok
                    - text: I domains by mutagenesis was reported (
                    - link "102" [ref=e324] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b102"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "103" [ref=e325] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b103"
                    - text: ). In theory, each of the zinc fingers bind to 3-bp-long DNA in a modular fashion (
                    - link "104" [ref=e326] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b104"
                    - text: ), and various zinc fingers generated by mutagenesis can be fused in tandem to generate zinc finger proteins targeting any of the desired sequences (
                    - link "105" [ref=e327] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b105"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "106" [ref=e328] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b106"
                    - text: ). In reality, however, the zinc finger proteins modularly assembled from each of the zinc fingers often show off-target effects (
                    - link "107" [ref=e329] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b107"
                    - text: ) or fail to target DNA (
                    - link "108" [ref=e330] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b108"
                    - text: ). There are several methods to select out nonfunctional ZFNs among the new assemblies (
                    - link "109" [ref=e331] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b109"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "110" [ref=e332] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b110"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "111" [ref=e333] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b111"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "112" [ref=e334] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b112"
                    - text: ); however, constructing a new functional ZFN is still a major challenge.
                  - 'figure "Tools for systems metabolic engineering. List of tools for genetic modification of candidate strains: recombineering, zinc finger nuclease (ZFN), transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN), clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 system, global transcription machinery engineering (gTME), omics-based tools, multiplex automated genome engineering (MAGE), synthetic small regulatory RNA (sRNA), and scaffold proteins." [ref=e335]':
                    - heading "Figure 2." [level=4] [ref=e336]
                    - paragraph [ref=e337]:
                      - img "Figure 2" [ref=e338]
                    - link "Open in a new tab" [ref=e340] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: figure/fig2/
                    - paragraph [ref=e342]:
                      - strong [ref=e343]: Tools for systems metabolic engineering.
                      - text: "List of tools for genetic modification of candidate strains: recombineering, zinc finger nuclease (ZFN), transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN), clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)/Cas9 system, global transcription machinery engineering (gTME), omics-based tools, multiplex automated genome engineering (MAGE), synthetic small regulatory RNA (sRNA), and scaffold proteins."
                - generic [ref=e344]:
                  - heading "Transcription Activator-Like Effector Nucleases (TALENs)" [level=3] [ref=e345]
                  - paragraph [ref=e346]:
                    - text: Despite the great modularity of ZFNs, the biggest weakness of this group of nucleases is twofold. First, a single zinc finger domain recognizes 3 bp at once (
                    - link "104" [ref=e347] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b104"
                    - text: ), requiring a library of at least 64 (=4
                    - superscript [ref=e348]: "3"
                    - text: ) modules for a complete coverage on all possible triplets of base pairs. The massive size of the library renders difficulties for several research groups from easily accessing the library, especially for those consisting of zinc finger domains with high sequence specificity. More importantly, the assembly of zinc finger proteins from each of the zinc finger modules often results in nonfunctional or erroneous products (
                    - link "107" [ref=e349] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b107"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "108" [ref=e350] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b108"
                    - text: ). An alternative engineered nuclease was developed to solve these problems with discovery of a group of proteins known as transcription activator-like effectors (TALEs). Initially discovered in plant pathogen
                    - emphasis [ref=e351]: Xanthomonas
                    - text: spp., TALEs are secreted from plant pathogens into the host cells and activate the transcription of plant genes, changing the physiology of the host plant (
                    - link "113" [ref=e352] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b113"
                    - text: ). A TALE consists of an array of 33 to 35 amino acids repeats, and each repeat specifically binds to a single nucleotide in the major groove (
                    - link "114" [ref=e353] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b114"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "115" [ref=e354] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b115"
                    - text: ). The 12th and 13th residues of each repeat, known as repeat variable diresidues (RVDs), determine the base pair specificities of each repeat (
                    - link "116" [ref=e355] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b116"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "117" [ref=e356] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b117"
                    - text: "). These properties indicate the superiority of TALEs over zinc finger proteins: TALEs require only four types of repeats that bind to each of the four types of base pairs, while zinc finger proteins need a set of 64 zinc fingers binding to 64 types of 3-bp-long DNA. After unraveling of RVDs in 2009, the application to use TALEs as programmable nucleases was quickly achieved in the very next year ("
                    - link "118" [ref=e357] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b118"
                    - text: ). Transcription activator-like effector nucleases (TALENs)—programmable nucleases based on TALEs—follow exactly the same scheme as that of ZFNs; the C-terminal nuclease domain of
                    - emphasis [ref=e358]: Fok
                    - text: I is fused to the C terminus of the TALE arrays (
                    - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e359] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig2"
                    - text: ). The use of up to 20 repeats in each TALEN, however, makes the construction of TALENs challenging—the repetitive occurrence of the homologous sequences in TALEN DNA constructs leads to instability of the constructs and their intermediates (
                    - link "119" [ref=e360] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b119"
                    - text: ). Nonetheless, attempts to improve the facile assembly of TALENs are continuing (
                    - link "120" [ref=e361] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b120"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "121" [ref=e362] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b121"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "122" [ref=e363] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b122"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "123" [ref=e364] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b123"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "124" [ref=e365] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b124"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "125" [ref=e366] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b125"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "126" [ref=e367] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b126"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e368]:
                  - heading "CRISPR/Cas System" [level=3] [ref=e369]
                  - paragraph [ref=e370]:
                    - text: In 2002, loci characterized by alternative occurrence of 21- to 37-bp-long repetitive sequences (repeats) and nonrepetitive sequences (spacers) were identified in prokaryotes by a bioinformatics analysis (
                    - link "127" [ref=e371] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b127"
                    - text: ). Reflecting the noticeable structural features of theses loci, they are named as clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPRs), although the initial observation was made in 1987 (
                    - link "128" [ref=e372] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b128"
                    - text: ). Moreover, protein-coding genes near CRISPRs were found together and named as CRISPR-associated (
                    - emphasis [ref=e373]: cas
                    - text: ) genes (
                    - link "127" [ref=e374] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b127"
                    - text: ). After the first discovery of CRISPR loci, many research groups suggested the role of CRISPR/Cas system as prokaryotic immunity (
                    - link "129" [ref=e375] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b129"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "130" [ref=e376] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b130"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "131" [ref=e377] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b131"
                    - text: ). In 2007, the suggested CRISPR’s role as a prokaryotic acquired immune system was confirmed (
                    - link "132" [ref=e378] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b132"
                    - text: ). The authors observed that
                    - emphasis [ref=e379]: Streptococcus thermophilus
                    - text: exposed to bacteriophages acquired new spacers derived from the phage DNA segments (later termed as protospacers) inside its CRISPR loci (
                    - link "132" [ref=e380] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b132"
                    - text: ). Moreover, modification of particular spacers in CRISPR modulated the resistance profile of the host cells against various bacteriophages, indicating close correlation between bacterial resistance against virus and the CRISPR/Cas system (
                    - link "132" [ref=e381] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b132"
                    - text: ). Subsequently, involvement of the CRISPR/Cas system in the resistance against plasmids and conjugation were also reported (
                    - link "133" [ref=e382] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b133"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "134" [ref=e383] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b134"
                    - text: ). After years of brilliant research, now it is understood that CRISPR loci are transcribed and the resulting CRISPR RNAs (crRNAs) are processed by several components including Cas proteins and RNase III (
                    - link "135" [ref=e384] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b135"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "136" [ref=e385] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b136"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "137" [ref=e386] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b137"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "138" [ref=e387] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b138"
                    - text: ). The processed crRNAs then work as effectors together with various other Cas proteins to cleave either DNA targets (
                    - link "135" [ref=e388] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b135"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "139" [ref=e389] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b139"
                    - text: ) or RNA targets (
                    - link "140" [ref=e390] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b140"
                    - text: "). When CRISPR/Cas systems are targeting their invader DNAs, they interrogate two points: the presence of protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)—the motif adjacent to protospacers that is required by effector Cas proteins to work as a nuclease—and complementarity of crRNA to the protospacer on target DNA ("
                    - link "141" [ref=e391] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b141"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "142" [ref=e392] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b142"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "143" [ref=e393] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b143"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e394]:
                    - text: "After years of efforts to classify various CRISPR/Cas systems, the systems are now categorized into five types, classified into two classes: type I, type III, and type IV in class 1 CRISPR/Cas system and type II and type V in class 2 CRISPR/Cas system ("
                    - link "144" [ref=e395] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b144"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "145" [ref=e396] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b145"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "146" [ref=e397] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b146"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "147" [ref=e398] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b147"
                    - text: ). Among three of them, Cas9 protein from
                    - emphasis [ref=e399]: Streptococcus pyogenes
                    - text: belonging to type II CRISPR/Cas system (
                    - link "148" [ref=e400] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b148"
                    - text: ), is especially the most widely used for genome engineering applications (
                    - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e401] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig2"
                    - text: ). In type II CRISPR/Cas system, crRNA are associated with
                    - emphasis [ref=e402]: trans
                    - text: "-activating crRNA (tracrRNA), and they together bind to the effector nuclease Cas9 ("
                    - link "148" [ref=e403] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b148"
                    - text: ). Elucidating the dual RNA systems in the CRISPR/Cas9 system, Doudna and her colleagues also created a chimeric guide RNA called single guide RNA (sgRNA) by joining essential motifs of crRNA and tracrRNA, making the system simpler (
                    - link "148" [ref=e404] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b148"
                    - text: ). Nowadays, both crRNA/tracrRNA and sgRNA systems are widely used for various applications. While meganucleases, ZFNs, and TALENs require the manipulation of effector proteins to program them to target genomic loci of interest, simple exchange of crRNA or sgRNA for the programming of CRISPR/Cas9 system led to a boom in the field of genome engineering. Although originated from prokaryotes, CRISPR/Cas9 systems are the most actively used in engineering of eukaryotic genomes (
                    - link "149" [ref=e405] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b149"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "150" [ref=e406] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b150"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "151" [ref=e407] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b151"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "152" [ref=e408] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b152"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "153" [ref=e409] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b153"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "154" [ref=e410] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b154"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "155" [ref=e411] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b155"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "156" [ref=e412] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b156"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "157" [ref=e413] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b157"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "158" [ref=e414] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b158"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "159" [ref=e415] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b159"
                    - text: ). There are relatively few examples of using CRISPR/Cas9 in prokaryotes (
                    - link "160" [ref=e416] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b160"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "161" [ref=e417] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b161"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "162" [ref=e418] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b162"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "163" [ref=e419] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b163"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "164" [ref=e420] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b164"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "165" [ref=e421] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b165"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "166" [ref=e422] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b166"
                    - text: ). The first example of using the CRISPR/Cas9 system in genome engineering of
                    - emphasis [ref=e423]: E. coli
                    - text: was reported by Marraffini and colleagues (
                    - link "160" [ref=e424] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b160"
                    - text: "). Their first trial utilized two plasmids: pCas9 containing tracrRNA, Cas9, and chloramphenicol resistance gene, and pCRISPR containing CRISPR spacer. Along with the application of recombineering strategy, these two plasmids and an oligo for point mutation were transformed, thus promoting successful recombination with a significant efficiency of 65 ± 14% ("
                    - link "160" [ref=e425] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b160"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e426]:
                    - text: The biggest concern in CRISPR/Cas9 systems is their off-target effects, as in other programmable nucleases. There have been many efforts to detect the off-target activity levels of the CRISPR/Cas9 systems (
                    - link "167" [ref=e427] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b167"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "168" [ref=e428] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b168"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "169" [ref=e429] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b169"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "170" [ref=e430] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b170"
                    - text: ). Moreover, many trials to reduce off-target activities have been reported, including the use of Cas9 nickases and catalytically dead Cas9 (dCas9)-
                    - emphasis [ref=e431]: Fok
                    - text: I nucleases (
                    - link "171" [ref=e432] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b171"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "172" [ref=e433] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b172"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "173" [ref=e434] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b173"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "174" [ref=e435] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b174"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "175" [ref=e436] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b175"
                    - text: ). In addition, the relatively big size of the Cas9 gene (approximately 4.2 kb) makes gene work on Cas9 more difficult. There is a recent report on an identification of smaller (around 3 kb in gene length) Cas9 from a multidrug-resistant
                    - emphasis [ref=e437]: Staphylococcus aureus
                    - text: (MRSA) isolated at an Irish hospital (
                    - link "176" [ref=e438] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b176"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e439]:
                  - heading "Repurposed CRISPR/Cas Systems" [level=3] [ref=e440]
                  - paragraph [ref=e441]:
                    - text: The CRISPR system not only has been a crucial genome-editing tool, but it also has been modified to be used as a
                    - emphasis [ref=e442]: trans
                    - text: "-acting gene knockdown system ("
                    - link "177" [ref=e443] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b177"
                    - text: "). The Cas9 protein with endonucleolytic activity was inactivated (dCas9) to repurpose this system into a gene expression regulating tool. This repurposed system knocks down gene expression by the following mechanism: when the target-oriented sgRNA and dCas9 are coexpressed, the scaffold of sgRNA binds with dCas9, leading the complex to the DNA sequence near the promoter site as in normal Cas9. After the complex binds the target DNA sequence, the CRISPRi R loop is formed, preventing the propagation of the incoming RNA polymerase and subsequently blocking the target gene transcription effectively. Fusing an activation domain or a repressor domain to dCas9 can be an alternative strategy for regulating gene expression using the CRISPR/Cas9 system. While this idea was successfully implemented in eukaryotic systems multiple times ("
                    - link "178" [ref=e444] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b178"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "179" [ref=e445] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b179"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "180" [ref=e446] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b180"
                    - text: ), only a single study reported to date has succeeded to activate a target gene with the dCas9-fusion protein system in
                    - emphasis [ref=e447]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "181" [ref=e448] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b181"
                    - text: ). The authors fused the omega subunit of RNA polymerase with dCas9 and targeted this complex upstream of the target gene promoter by engineering the corresponding crRNA. The authors tested this system for overexpressing
                    - emphasis [ref=e449]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. lacZ" [ref=e450] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10527
                    - text: ", which encodes beta-galactosidase, and obtained a 2.8-fold increase in expression when the omega subunit was fused to dCas9 at its C terminus."
                - generic [ref=e451]:
                  - heading "Small Regulatory RNAs" [level=3] [ref=e452]
                  - paragraph [ref=e453]:
                    - text: While there have been significant advances in the regulation of gene expression by means of developing promoter, ribosome binding site, or intergenic regions between genes in a single operon for fine-tuning of gene expression, modification in chromosomal DNA is not only time consuming and laborious, but also unfit for engineering multiple targets simultaneously (
                    - link "182" [ref=e454] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b182"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "183" [ref=e455] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b183"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "184" [ref=e456] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b184"
                    - text: ). As such, a new method for simultaneously studying multiple genes using
                    - emphasis [ref=e457]: trans
                    - text: "-acting small regulatory RNAs (sRNA) for regulation and fine-tuning of inherent genes in"
                    - emphasis [ref=e458]: E. coli
                    - text: was developed (
                    - link "185" [ref=e459] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b185"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "186" [ref=e460] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b186"
                    - text: ). This strategy derives from native sRNAs in bacteria regulating gene expression by translational control (
                    - link "187" [ref=e461] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b187"
                    - text: "). The structure of synthetic sRNA construct consists of three major constituents: a target-binding sequence, scaffold, and terminator ("
                    - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e462] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig2"
                    - text: ). sRNAs regulate gene expression by base-pairing its sequences to the target translation initiation region, consequently blocking the ribosome from taking action and thus significantly reducing translation efficiency (
                    - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e463] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig2"
                    - text: ). The target-binding sequence is engineered into the antisense sequence (24 bp) of the translation initiation region of the target gene to be regulated. The scaffold within sRNA binds to an RNA chaperone Hfq protein, so as to enhance the binding of sRNA to the target mRNA sequence and to catalyze the degradation of mRNA by recruiting RNase E (
                    - link "187" [ref=e464] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b187"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "188" [ref=e465] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b188"
                    - text: ). Among the 101
                    - emphasis [ref=e466]: E. coli
                    - text: sRNAs discovered recently, the scaffold of MicC was selected for its strong repression capability. The advantages of using synthetic sRNAs as a tool is in its ability to test knockdown of essential genes and to fine-tune gene expressions, its ease in vector construction thus expediting the experiment process, and its ability to target multiple sites simultaneously. It has also been reported that not only repression, but also activation of certain genes by means of sRNAs exist in nature (
                    - link "189" [ref=e467] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b189"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "190" [ref=e468] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b190"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e469]:
                  - heading "Global Transcription Machinery Engineering (gTME)" [level=3] [ref=e470]
                  - paragraph [ref=e471]:
                    - text: After decades of extensive study on genotypes and phenotypes of various biological systems, it is now widely accepted that a majority of phenotypes are polygenic, rather than monogenic. Hence, an ability to simultaneously select and adjust multiple genes is very critical to engineer organisms for a desired trait, especially in the field of metabolic engineering. Intuition- and logic-based target gene selection to engineer a single phenotype is limited in many situations. Simultaneous manipulation of multiple target genes chosen is not affordable with traditional gene/genome engineering tools, either. In such situations, mimicking nature’s strategy to develop novel systems or components can be a wise choice—evolution, a series of random mutagenesis and selection. Stephanopoulos and colleagues introduced a concept named global transcription machinery engineering (gTME) that targets components in global transcription regulation for random mutagenesis to randomly manipulate gene expression profile in a transcriptome-wide manner followed by an application of proper selection powers (
                    - link "191" [ref=e472] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b191"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "192" [ref=e473] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b192"
                    - text: ). They proved the system both in a eukaryotic microorganism yeast (
                    - link "191" [ref=e474] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b191"
                    - text: ) and in a prokaryote
                    - emphasis [ref=e475]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "192" [ref=e476] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b192"
                    - text: ). In gTME application in
                    - emphasis [ref=e477]: E. coli
                    - text: ", one or multiple components involved in global transcription regulation, such as"
                    - emphasis [ref=e478]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. rpoD" [ref=e479] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10896
                    - text: ", are initially selected for construction of mutant libraries. The mutant libraries generated are then introduced into a host microorganism in the presence of a corresponding, nonmutagenized component. Subsequently, an individual organism exhibiting desired traits such as tolerance is selected by applying the proper screening method to the host containing the mutant libraries of the target global transcriptional constituents. The strength of gTME is that it enables engineering of multiple target genes, which are not often intuitive or logical, for desired phenotypes in a short period ("
                    - link "191" [ref=e480] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b191"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "192" [ref=e481] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b192"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e482]:
                  - heading "Multiplex Automated Genome Engineering (MAGE)" [level=3] [ref=e483]
                  - paragraph [ref=e484]:
                    - text: Instead of creating mutant global transcription factors for genome engineering, direct multiplex editing of genomic loci can also be achieved. Church and his colleagues provided the way to simultaneously manipulate multiple genomic loci either randomly or rationally mutagenized (
                    - link "53" [ref=e485] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b53"
                    - text: ). Unlike gTME, where transcriptome profiles are altered by mutant global transcription machineries, MAGE can generate a library of hosts with multiple genomic loci edited directly in the genomic sequence where the editing includes residue substitution, deletion, and insertion. With bacteriophage λ Red ssDNA binding protein β expressed, mutation-containing ssDNA oligonucleotides for targeting the lagging strand of replication fork during DNA replication at designated genomic loci are introduced into a host by electrophoresis, generating a daughter population of hosts containing targeted sequences edited. A pool of various oligonucleotides can be delivered into the host at once, and repeated delivery of the oligo library results in a set of hosts with genomic sequences differentially modified in each generation. It is noticeable that the whole procedure of repetitive oligo delivery is automatically operated with the help of machinery and an operating program developed in the research (
                    - link "53" [ref=e486] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b53"
                    - text: ). Once experimental conditions are optimized, more than 30% of the host population incorporates mutation for a single locus, which only takes 2 to 2.5 h (
                    - link "53" [ref=e487] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b53"
                    - text: ). Modified versions of MAGE for improved modification efficiency have also been reported (
                    - link "193" [ref=e488] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b193"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "194" [ref=e489] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b194"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e490]:
                  - heading "Conjugative Assembly Genome Engineering (CAGE)" [level=3] [ref=e491]
                  - paragraph [ref=e492]:
                    - text: While recombinant plasmids can be transferred among strains after they are constructed in one host strain, modifications made directly on genomic DNA, however, are hard coded and difficult to be transferred in parallel. In order to reintroduce the same chromosomal modifications in a different strain, the same modification procedures must be performed repeatedly. This makes parallel genomic modification-based engineering inefficient and time consuming compared with plasmid-based engineering. In 2011, Church group reported genome-wide substitution of every TGA stop codon to TAA by accumulating pieces of partial genomic modifications made on each host cell line into a single, final host strain (
                    - link "195" [ref=e493] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b195"
                    - text: ). They named the system employed for this achievement as conjugative assembly genome engineering (CAGE), which literally describes the core mechanism involved in this system.
                  - paragraph [ref=e494]:
                    - text: CAGE maximally utilizes the virtue of DNA transfer from one cell to another during a process called conjugation. Isaacs et al. split the F
                    - superscript [ref=e495]: +
                    - text: "plasmid, which enables the host cell working as a donor cell during conjugation, into two parts:"
                    - emphasis [ref=e496]: oriT
                    - text: and the other constituents.
                    - emphasis [ref=e497]: oriT
                    - text: ", the starting point of DNA replication and subsequent transfer of F"
                    - superscript [ref=e498]: +
                    - text: plasmid to a recipient cell during conjugation, is integrated into the host genome to make the host competent for a donor role (
                    - link "195" [ref=e499] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b195"
                    - text: ). This causes the whole genomic DNA to be replicated and transferred to the recipient cell during conjugation. The remaining components in F
                    - superscript [ref=e500]: +
                    - text: plasmid, in contrast, are retained as a closed-circular plasmid and introduced to the donor cell during CAGE process. While they help the process of conjugation, they are not transferred to the recipient since they are physically separated from
                    - emphasis [ref=e501]: oriT
                    - text: . The prepared donor cells are then cocultured with recipient cells, promoting conjugation between two different cell populations to transfer the modified genomic DNA from donors to the recipients. Subsequently, the transferred donor genomic DNA substitutes the corresponding region in recipient genome with the help of recipient cell’s endogenous recombination machinery (
                    - link "195" [ref=e502] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b195"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e503]:
                    - text: The recombination, however, is a stochastic process and the points where recombination occurs are randomly chosen. Consequently, the probability for a locus on donor genomic DNA to replace the corresponding recipient DNA segment is higher as the locus is located further from both ends of the linearized donor DNA fragment, following simple probability theories. To make sure the engineered regions on donor genomic DNA successfully substitutes the recipient DNA, the engineered region on donor cells is bounded by
                    - emphasis [ref=e504]: oriT
                    - text: and a positive selection marker, including antibiotic resistance genes (
                    - link "195" [ref=e505] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b195"
                    - text: ). Moreover, the starting point of a region to be replaced on recipient genome is defined by a positive-negative selection marker, such as
                    - emphasis [ref=e506]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. tolC" [ref=e507] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11009
                    - text: (
                    - link "196" [ref=e508] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b196"
                    - text: ) and
                    - emphasis [ref=e509]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. galK" [ref=e510] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10363
                    - text: (
                    - link "45" [ref=e511] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b45"
                    - text: ). Together with these markers, resulting recombinant cells with the first recombination point occurring too far away from
                    - emphasis [ref=e512]: oriT
                    - text: are selected out by negative selection effect of the positive-negative marker. On the other hand, ones with the second recombination occurring too close to the first recombination site are selected out since they cannot survive without a positive marker. In this manner, the only final recombinant strains containing the whole engineered segment of the donor genome are obtainable. These processes can be repeated until all of the pieces of partially engineered regions of each cell line are accumulated in a single cell line.
                - generic [ref=e513]:
                  - heading "Trackable Multiplex Recombineering (TRMR)" [level=3] [ref=e514]
