                  - paragraph [ref=e515]:
                    - text: The random engineering of multiple genomic loci allows isolation of new strains with unexpected target genes modified in an unexpected way. Obtaining such a brand new strain itself is a great work, but it will be more amazing to know how the new strain is changed. A method called trackable multiplex recombineering (TRMR), suggested by Warner et al., provides a way to manipulate multiple genomic loci, detect the loci affected, and elucidate the manner in which they are modified (
                    - link "197" [ref=e516] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b197"
                    - text: ). In TRMR, 20-bp-long “barcode sequences” are inserted upstream or downstream of the target genomic loci while the target loci are simultaneously modified with the help of the recombineering techniques. The barcodes are used for detecting the changes that occurred at the target loci. Combined with microarray techniques, they can give information on allelic frequencies of the modified genes in a bacterial population subjected to TRMR (
                    - link "197" [ref=e517] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b197"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "198" [ref=e518] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b198"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e519]:
                  - heading "Synthetic Scaffolds and Bacterial Microcompartments" [level=3] [ref=e520]
                  - paragraph [ref=e521]:
                    - text: The idea of spatial organization of enzymes was first conceived from mammalian signal transduction pathways where grouping of enzymes by spatial organization is needed to handle signal transductions from one billion proteins (
                    - link "199" [ref=e522] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b199"
                    - text: ); similarly, metabolism within a cell is a highly complex network of chemical reactions. With this complexity, problems may occur in regard to unwanted side reactions (
                    - link "200" [ref=e523] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b200"
                    - text: ), limiting metabolic flux due to low substrate specificity (
                    - link "201" [ref=e524] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b201"
                    - text: ), low productivity and yield (
                    - link "9" [ref=e525] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b9"
                    - text: ), and hindrance of cell growth by toxic materials (
                    - link "202" [ref=e526] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b202"
                    - text: ). Handling these problems would require channeling of substrates or directing target chemicals or enzymes to a confined area. To cope with these problems, examples from nature were readily adopted (
                    - link "203" [ref=e527] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b203"
                    - text: ), which include tryptophan synthase inherent in
                    - emphasis [ref=e528]: Salmonella enterica
                    - text: serovar Typhimurium (
                    - link "204" [ref=e529] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b204"
                    - text: ), carbamoyl phosphate synthetase, and glutamine phosphoribosylpyrophosphate aminotransferase in
                    - emphasis [ref=e530]: E. coli
                    - text: ", and dihydrofolate reductase-thymidylate synthase inherent in"
                    - emphasis [ref=e531]: Leishmania major
                    - text: (
                    - link "205" [ref=e532] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b205"
                    - text: ). Additionally, carboxysomes were discovered and characterized in cyanobacteria and chemolithotrophic bacterial species, in which rate-limiting steps involved in the Calvin cycle take place (
                    - link "206" [ref=e533] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b206"
                    - text: ). Inspired by these examples, synthetic scaffolds and bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) were developed. Synthetic scaffolds aim at localizing enzymes in order to increase the local intermediate concentration of a desired biochemical reaction or to prevent toxic materials from damaging the cell. Starting from the development of synthetic protein scaffold (
                    - link "201" [ref=e534] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b201"
                    - text: ), synthetic scaffolds using RNA (
                    - link "207" [ref=e535] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b207"
                    - text: ) and DNA (
                    - link "208" [ref=e536] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b208"
                    - text: ) as building blocks were sequentially developed, all of which were demonstrated in
                    - emphasis [ref=e537]: E. coli
                    - text: .
                  - paragraph [ref=e538]:
                    - text: BMCs, which resemble organelles within eukaryotic cells, tend to encapsulate large numbers of certain enzymes to form distinct reaction environments. This tendency increases the concentration of intermediates such as in carboxysome, in which CO
                    - subscript [ref=e539]: "2"
                    - text: is concentrated around the otherwise inefficient RuBisCO (
                    - link "209" [ref=e540] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b209"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "210" [ref=e541] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b210"
                    - text: ). Additionally, toxic intermediates are effectively blocked from incorporating into the host metabolism as in examples of Eut and Pdu microcompartments (
                    - link "211" [ref=e542] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b211"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "212" [ref=e543] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b212"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "213" [ref=e544] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b213"
                    - text: ). It is interesting to note that BMCs are thought to regulate the amount and types of chemicals that can go through the compartment, while intermediates and toxic materials seemed to be kept inside of the bacterial microcompartments (BMCs), nontoxic native substrates, and products diffuse across the compartment relatively easily (
                    - link "210" [ref=e545] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b210"
                    - text: ). The precise mechanism of how this happens is yet to be determined, although several hypotheses exist (
                    - link "212" [ref=e546] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b212"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "214" [ref=e547] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b214"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "215" [ref=e548] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b215"
                    - text: ). Encapsulins and lumazine synthase complexes are two other simpler microcompartment systems reported (
                    - link "216" [ref=e549] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b216"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "217" [ref=e550] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b217"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e551]:
                  - heading "Omics Tools" [level=3] [ref=e552]
                  - paragraph [ref=e553]:
                    - text: In systems metabolic engineering, omics-based tools are system-wide strategies that utilize data from x-omes to analyze hosts on the systems level and unravel unknown mechanisms to enhance the production of target chemicals. Since a tremendous amount of data is associated with multiomics-based approaches, computational simulations often aid in the omics analysis. Readers are encouraged to refer to several excellent reviews on multiomics studies and incorporation of
                    - emphasis [ref=e554]: in silico
                    - text: simulations (
                    - link "218" [ref=e555] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b218"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "219" [ref=e556] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b219"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "220" [ref=e557] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b220"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "221" [ref=e558] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b221"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e559]:
                    - text: The first bacterial genome sequencing of
                    - emphasis [ref=e560]: Haemophilus influenzae
                    - text: opened the field of genomics, starting a new era in omics-based approaches (
                    - link "222" [ref=e561] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b222"
                    - text: ). Numerous sequencing technologies have emerged since this first onset, facilitating the development of genomics (
                    - link "223" [ref=e562] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b223"
                    - text: ). With the increasing amount of genome data, comparative genomics comparing the genome sequences of two organisms has become feasible. From the genomic data open and available for all, genome-scale modeling has been developed actively, which will be explained in later sections (
                    - link "224" [ref=e563] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b224"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "225" [ref=e564] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b225"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "226" [ref=e565] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b226"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e566]:
                    - text: However, the expression levels of each gene cannot be identified through genomics. Transcriptomics analyzes the mRNA levels of various genes at a time, particularly the change of gene expression levels when given perturbation (
                    - link "218" [ref=e567] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b218"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "227" [ref=e568] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b227"
                    - text: ). The development of transcriptomics has had a deep relationship with the development of high-throughput microarray development (
                    - link "228" [ref=e569] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b228"
                    - text: ). By measuring the fluorescence in the microarray, the expression levels of each gene can be examined. For transcriptome modeling, a reverse-engineering strategy named network identification by regression (NIR) was used (
                    - link "229" [ref=e570] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b229"
                    - text: ). Transcriptomics has several applications, such as the elucidation of useful metabolic genes (
                    - link "230" [ref=e571] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b230"
                    - text: ) or the identification of target genes or pathways to be engineered (
                    - link "231" [ref=e572] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b231"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e573]:
                    - text: Unlike transcriptome, proteome reflects the posttranscriptional regulations by small RNAs, mRNA degradation, and represents the real phenotype of the cell much more clearly than the transcriptome does. Readers are invited to read an excellent review on the proteome of
                    - emphasis [ref=e574]: E. coli
                    - text: covering aspects not explained in this section (
                    - link "232" [ref=e575] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b232"
                    - text: ). Two-dimensional (2D) electrophoresis is a widely used method for analyzing an organism’s proteome (
                    - link "233" [ref=e576] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b233"
                    - text: ). For highly expressed proteins, however, biased results were often shown (
                    - link "234" [ref=e577] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b234"
                    - text: ), leading to the development of non-gel-based approaches such as mass spectrometry (MS) (
                    - link "235" [ref=e578] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b235"
                    - text: ), matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization–time of flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) (
                    - link "236" [ref=e579] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b236"
                    - text: ), and liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) (
                    - link "237" [ref=e580] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b237"
                    - text: ). The main interest in proteomics analysis is to examine the change in cellular and metabolic states during the production of metabolites of interest.
                  - paragraph [ref=e581]:
                    - text: Since the proteome of an organism still does not precisely represent the physiology of the cell and enzyme activities, additional omics was needed, leading to the emergence of metabolomics (
                    - link "238" [ref=e582] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b238"
                    - text: ). Several analytical methods were adopted for metabolomic analyses including nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) (
                    - link "239" [ref=e583] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b239"
                    - text: ), high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (
                    - link "240" [ref=e584] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b240"
                    - text: ), and MS (
                    - link "241" [ref=e585] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b241"
                    - text: ). Metabolomics, however, contains a serious problem arising from the dynamic turnover events of cellular metabolites. Therefore, an instant quenching method is required (
                    - link "242" [ref=e586] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b242"
                    - text: ). Other problems such as cultivation techniques and metabolite extraction methods are some of the ongoing challenges.
                  - paragraph [ref=e587]:
                    - text: Fluxomics is widely modeled and applied in metabolic engineering, because it analyzes the reaction rates of different metabolic pathways (
                    - link "243" [ref=e588] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b243"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "244" [ref=e589] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b244"
                    - text: "). Because it is almost impossible to obtain the dynamic intracellular fluxes of a cellular system, indirect approaches are used for metabolic flux analysis (MFA):"
                    - superscript [ref=e590]: "13"
                    - text: C-based flux analysis and constraints-based flux analysis. The basic assumption in these analyses is that the cellular fluxes are at steady state. In
                    - superscript [ref=e591]: "13"
                    - text: C-based analysis, an isotope-labeled carbon source is fed to the medium, letting
                    - superscript [ref=e592]: "13"
                    - text: C-incorporated metabolites to be detected and patterns to be analyzed by NMR and gas chromatography mass spectrometry (GC/MS) (
                    - link "245" [ref=e593] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b245"
                    - text: ). However, expensive isotope samples, difficulty in conducting experiments, and large-scale calculations are the bottlenecks in this approach. Constraints-based flux analysis is a set of algorithms for optimization-based simulation (
                    - link "246" [ref=e594] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b246"
                    - text: ). Metabolic flux analysis can also be used for elucidating the metabolic characteristics of a newly identified organism such as in the case of
                    - emphasis [ref=e595]: Mannheimia succiniciproducens
                    - text: (
                    - link "247" [ref=e596] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b247"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e597]:
                    - text: Other kinds of omics including glycomics, lipidomics, and interactomics have also been actively researched to date. Because each omics study has its own drawbacks, the integrated analysis and use of omics are required for a comprehensive analysis of an organism. The first attempt to integrate multiple omics was by Hood and colleagues to characterize the phenotype of
                    - emphasis [ref=e598]: S. cerevisiae
                    - text: (
                    - link "248" [ref=e599] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b248"
                    - text: ). Several other significant multiomics studies regarding
                    - emphasis [ref=e600]: E. coli
                    - text: are as listed (
                    - link "249" [ref=e601] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b249"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "250" [ref=e602] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b250"
                    - text: ). A prominent tool that deals with the multiomics data of
                    - emphasis [ref=e603]: E. coli
                    - text: is EcoCyc (
                    - link "251" [ref=e604] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b251"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "252" [ref=e605] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b252"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "253" [ref=e606] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b253"
                    - text: ). Through the latest version of EcoCyc, a tremendous amount of data including genes, metabolites, reactions, operons, metabolic pathways, and metabolic flux models of
                    - emphasis [ref=e607]: E. coli
                    - text: can be accessed (
                    - link "253" [ref=e608] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b253"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e609]:
                  - heading "In Silico Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Models and Tools" [level=3] [ref=e610]:
                    - emphasis [ref=e611]: In Silico
                    - text: Genome-Scale Metabolic Network Models and Tools
                  - paragraph [ref=e612]:
                    - text: A massive amount of genome data has been accumulating since the beginning of the genomic era. The availability of such information allowed researchers to understand and predict the physiology of organisms. One of the initial studies used such information to predict the growth of bacteria (
                    - link "254" [ref=e613] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b254"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "255" [ref=e614] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b255"
                    - text: ). Currently, these data are routinely applied to predict and analyze detailed physiological and metabolic status of bacteria (
                    - link "22" [ref=e615] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b22"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "25" [ref=e616] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b25"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "225" [ref=e617] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b225"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "256" [ref=e618] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b256"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "257" [ref=e619] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b257"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "258" [ref=e620] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b258"
                    - text: ). There are several comprehensive reviews covering the diverse applications of genome data for various purposes (
                    - link "259" [ref=e621] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b259"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "260" [ref=e622] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b260"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "261" [ref=e623] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b261"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "262" [ref=e624] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b262"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "263" [ref=e625] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b263"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e626]:
                    - text: A single genome-scale metabolic network model consists of an immense amount of data from various literature, experimental sets, and databases. The data integrated into a single genome-scale model includes information on genome-wide metabolic genes, hundreds to thousands of metabolites, and thousands of stoichiometric metabolic reactions. Constructing such models is beyond the scope of this review, and descriptions of the methods to construct such models can be found from other reviews and book chapters (
                    - link "259" [ref=e627] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b259"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "260" [ref=e628] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b260"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "264" [ref=e629] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b264"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "265" [ref=e630] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b265"
                    - text: ). During past three decades of
                    - emphasis [ref=e631]: E. coli
                    - text: genome-scale reconstruction history, several versions of thorough
                    - emphasis [ref=e632]: E. coli
                    - text: genome-scale metabolic network models have been published (
                    - link "225" [ref=e633] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b225"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "256" [ref=e634] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b256"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "257" [ref=e635] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b257"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "266" [ref=e636] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b266"
                    - text: ), such as EcoMBEL979 (
                    - link "266" [ref=e637] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b266"
                    - text: ),
                    - emphasis [ref=e638]: i
                    - text: AF1260 (
                    - link "225" [ref=e639] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b225"
                    - text: ),
                    - emphasis [ref=e640]: i
                    - text: JO1366 (
                    - link "256" [ref=e641] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b256"
                    - text: ), and EcoCyc-18.0-GEM (
                    - link "267" [ref=e642] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b267"
                    - text: ) containing thousands of metabolites, metabolic enzymes, and stoichiometric reaction rulesets.
                  - paragraph [ref=e643]:
                    - text: An
                    - emphasis [ref=e644]: E. coli
                    - text: genome-scale model alone cannot exhibit the metabolic state of this bacterium in a given condition. To determine the metabolic state, flux information of each metabolic reaction should be determined. However, there are many more metabolic reactions than metabolites in the models, as in real
                    - emphasis [ref=e645]: E. coli
                    - text: ", rendering the complete determination of the exact flux solutions impossible; for example, the most thorough"
                    - emphasis [ref=e646]: E. coli
                    - text: K-12 MG1655 genome-scale model,
                    - emphasis [ref=e647]: i
                    - text: JO1366, contains 1,136 metabolites and 1,473 metabolic reactions (
                    - link "256" [ref=e648] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b256"
                    - text: ). In bacteria, the complex sets of regulatory components fine-tune the metabolic fluxes. In current
                    - emphasis [ref=e649]: E. coli
                    - text: genome-scale models, unfortunately, such complicated regulations have not been implemented yet. Therefore, during
                    - emphasis [ref=e650]: in silico
                    - text: simulations, an algorithm mimicking or representing such regulations should be employed to select the best prediction on the real metabolic state among the vast solution space.
                  - paragraph [ref=e651]:
                    - text: Flux balance analysis (FBA) is the most widely used algorithm. Based on genome-scale models, FBA applies stoichiometric information as major constraints and builds a solution space for metabolic flux distribution (
                    - link "255" [ref=e652] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b255"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "268" [ref=e653] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b268"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "269" [ref=e654] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b269"
                    - text: ). To specify a solution that best represents the actual state among the possible solutions, FBA generally employs an objective function of maximum biomass formation. This is based on the assumption that
                    - emphasis [ref=e655]: E. coli
                    - text: and other bacteria have evolved to maximize their growth and replication, reflecting the generally acknowledged expression “The goal of every bacterium is to become bacteria” as said by microbiologist Stanley Falkow. Simulation of how a genetic perturbation modulates the flux distribution is also an important aspect in metabolic engineering, especially for the selection of engineering targets. In addition to FBA, another useful algorithm for this purpose is the minimization of metabolic adjustment (MOMA) algorithm (
                    - link "270" [ref=e656] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b270"
                    - text: ). This algorithm is based on the idea that when perturbation is introduced in a bacterial strain by knocking out one or more genes, the bacteria redistribute their metabolic fluxes to minimize flux changes (
                    - link "270" [ref=e657] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b270"
                    - text: ). Based on the reference flux distribution data obtained from FBA, MOMA can be employed to predict modifications in the flux distribution. The third noticeable algorithm is the regulatory on/off minimization (ROOM) algorithm (
                    - link "271" [ref=e658] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b271"
                    - text: ). This algorithm is similar to MOMA, but differs in that ROOM focuses on minimizing the number of fluxes significantly changed, i.e., turned on or off, while MOMA focuses on minimizing the total magnitude of changes throughout the whole metabolic fluxes (
                    - link "271" [ref=e659] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b271"
                    - text: ). All these algorithms predict the physiology of bacteria fairly well, and each has its strengths and weaknesses in different conditions, such as initial stages or steady-state phases (
                    - link "271" [ref=e660] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b271"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e661]:
                    - text: These genome-scale metabolic models and metabolic state prediction algorithms can be used together to select engineering targets for improving strain performances. For these purposes, several algorithms have been developed and reported. These include OptForce (
                    - link "272" [ref=e662] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b272"
                    - text: ), OptKnock (
                    - link "273" [ref=e663] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b273"
                    - text: ), OptGene (
                    - link "274" [ref=e664] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b274"
                    - text: ), OptSwap (
                    - link "275" [ref=e665] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b275"
                    - text: ), FSEOF (flux scanning based on enforced objective flux) (
                    - link "258" [ref=e666] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b258"
                    - text: ), FVSEOF (flux variability scanning based on enforced objective flux) (
                    - link "276" [ref=e667] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b276"
                    - text: ), and CosMos (
                    - link "277" [ref=e668] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b277"
                    - text: ). Most algorithms contain one of the three metabolic flux prediction algorithms FBA, MOMA, and ROOM within. Moreover, there are numerous environments for
                    - emphasis [ref=e669]: in silico
                    - text: simulation, such as MatLab-based COBRA Toolbox (
                    - link "278" [ref=e670] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b278"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "279" [ref=e671] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b279"
                    - text: ) and a stand-alone program suite MetaFluxNet (
                    - link "280" [ref=e672] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b280"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "281" [ref=e673] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b281"
                    - text: ). With the help of these models, algorithms, and programs, targets of gene knockout, amplification, and flux level adjustment to improve strains can be predicted.
                  - paragraph [ref=e674]:
                    - text: Design and construction of novel biosynthetic pathways can also be assisted by
                    - emphasis [ref=e675]: in silico
                    - text: "pathway prediction tools. Such algorithms consist of two components: reaction rule sets and heuristics for narrowing down most probable pathway candidates. Currently, numerous pathway prediction tools are available for designing novel biosynthetic pathways for chemicals of interest, including PathoLogic ("
                    - link "282" [ref=e676] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b282"
                    - text: ), PathMiner (
                    - link "283" [ref=e677] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b283"
                    - text: ), BNICE (
                    - link "284" [ref=e678] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b284"
                    - text: ), Pathway Hunter Tool (
                    - link "285" [ref=e679] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b285"
                    - text: ), DESHARKY (
                    - link "286" [ref=e680] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b286"
                    - text: ), UM-PPS (
                    - link "287" [ref=e681] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b287"
                    - text: ), MetaRoute (
                    - link "288" [ref=e682] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b288"
                    - text: ), Rahnuma (
                    - link "289" [ref=e683] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b289"
                    - text: ), ReTrace (
                    - link "290" [ref=e684] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b290"
                    - text: ), Atom Metanet (
                    - link "291" [ref=e685] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b291"
                    - text: ), Cho et al. 2010 (
                    - link "292" [ref=e686] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b292"
                    - text: ), PathPred (
                    - link "293" [ref=e687] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b293"
                    - text: ), RetroPath (
                    - link "294" [ref=e688] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b294"
                    - text: ), SymPheny Biopathway Predictor (
                    - link "27" [ref=e689] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b27"
                    - text: ), XTMS (
                    - link "295" [ref=e690] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b295"
                    - text: ), GEM-Path (
                    - link "296" [ref=e691] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b296"
                    - text: ), and RouteSearch (
                    - link "297" [ref=e692] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b297"
                    - text: ). There are a number of indepth reviews describing and analyzing such useful tools (
                    - link "259" [ref=e693] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b259"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "260" [ref=e694] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b260"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "261" [ref=e695] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b261"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "262" [ref=e696] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b262"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "263" [ref=e697] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b263"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "298" [ref=e698] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b298"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "300" [ref=e699] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b300"
                    - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e700]:
                  - heading "Plasmid Addiction System" [level=3] [ref=e701]
                  - paragraph [ref=e702]:
                    - text: Selection for plasmid-transformed bacteria has been the foundation in development of biotechnology, and the use of plasmids for industrial application is ever crucial (
                    - link "301" [ref=e703] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b301"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "302" [ref=e704] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b302"
                    - text: ). The plasmid-harboring bacteria are often selected in the presence of antibiotics. However, the use of antibiotics for industrial-scale systems is often undesired due in part to the cost of antibiotics, contamination of products with residual antibiotics, and possible degradation of antibiotics leading to instability of plasmids during cultivation (
                    - link "303" [ref=e705] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b303"
                    - text: ). In light of problems with antibiotics in industrial systems, the plasmid addiction system delivers an alternative mode of selection while maintaining plasmids in an antibiotics-free environment.
                  - paragraph [ref=e706]:
                    - text: "The plasmid addiction system can be largely categorized into three types: toxin/antitoxin-based, metabolism-based, or operator repressor titration systems ("
                    - link "301" [ref=e707] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b301"
                    - text: ). An example for the toxin/antitoxin-based system adapted from phage P1 protein called Doc (death on curing) and Phd (prevent host death) where the former is toxin and latter is antitoxin (
                    - link "304" [ref=e708] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b304"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "305" [ref=e709] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b305"
                    - text: ). The toxin is stable and causes cell death in the absence of plasmid, whereas the unstable antitoxin prevents cell death in the presence of plasmid. Cell propagation thus only depends on the presence of plasmid, which harbors both toxin and antitoxin, where the latter inhibits the activity of the former. In the operator repressor titration system, a gene essential for metabolism, such as
                    - emphasis [ref=e710]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. dapD" [ref=e711] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10207
                    - text: ", is controlled under the"
                    - emphasis [ref=e712]: lac
                    - text: operator/promoter (
                    - link "306" [ref=e713] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b306"
                    - text: ). Repression of
                    - emphasis [ref=e714]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. dapD" [ref=e715] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10207
                    - text: expression prevents L-lysine biosynthesis and peptidoglycan chain cross-linking (
                    - link "307" [ref=e716] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b307"
                    - text: ). The host
                    - emphasis [ref=e717]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. lacI" [ref=e718] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10525
                    - text: repressor thus inhibits growth unless it is sequestered or “titrated” away from the
                    - emphasis [ref=e719]: lac
                    - text: operator/promoter controlling
                    - emphasis [ref=e720]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. dapD" [ref=e721] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10207
                    - text: expression. This titration is achieved by introducing another
                    - emphasis [ref=e722]: lac
                    - text: operator/promoter on a multicopy plasmid (
                    - link "303" [ref=e723] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b303"
                    - text: ). Similarly, an essential gene for cell growth and metabolism is deleted in the host chromosome in the metabolism-based system. (
                    - link "308" [ref=e724] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b308"
                    - text: ). A notable study using this system involves the deletion of
                    - emphasis [ref=e725]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. dapE" [ref=e726] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10208
                    - text: in the host chromosome and complementing it with
                    - emphasis [ref=e727]: dapL
                    - text: from
                    - emphasis [ref=e728]: Synechocystis
                    - text: sp. PCC 6308 (
                    - link "301" [ref=e729] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b301"
                    - text: ). Using this strategy, the transformed
                    - emphasis [ref=e730]: E. coli
                    - text: was able to maintain the plasmid during cultivation at a 400-liter fermentation in a 650-liter tank for cyanophycin production. The plasmid stability reported here is at 98%, and up to 18% (w/w) of dry cell weight (DCW) for the polymer was demonstrated. It must be noted that this study serves as an important example in the field of systems metabolic engineering for producing value-added chemicals at a semi-industrial scale without any antibiotics (
                    - link "301" [ref=e731] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b301"
                    - text: ).
              - generic [ref=e732]:
                - heading "STRATEGIES FOR SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF E. COLI" [level=2] [ref=e733]:
                  - text: STRATEGIES FOR SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF
                  - emphasis [ref=e734]: E. COLI
                - paragraph [ref=e735]:
                  - text: The hallmark of systems metabolic engineering is to produce desired chemicals with engineered microbes not only to industrial-scale standards, but also to bring changes imperative to the chemical industry. To achieve such goals, various strategies described here have been developed to engineer both native and synthetic pathways of
                  - emphasis [ref=e736]: E. coli
                  - text: for the production of valuable chemicals (
                  - link "Fig. 3" [ref=e737] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#fig3"
                  - text: ). The strategies described here utilize various tools including those listed in the previous section.
                  - link "Table 1" [ref=e738] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: "#T1"
                  - text: summarizes notable achievements in the production of valuable chemicals in
                  - emphasis [ref=e739]: E. coli
                  - text: strains with metabolic engineering strategies described in genotypic notation.
                - figure [ref=e740]:
                  - heading "Figure 3." [level=3] [ref=e741]
                  - paragraph [ref=e742]:
                    - img "Figure 3" [ref=e743]
                  - link "Open in a new tab" [ref=e745] [cursor=pointer]:
                    - /url: figure/fig3/
                  - paragraph [ref=e747]:
                    - strong [ref=e748]:
                      - text: The endogenous metabolism of
                      - emphasis [ref=e749]: E. coli
                      - text: .
                    - text: The endogenous metabolic pathway of
                    - emphasis [ref=e750]: E. coli
                    - text: mapping products (metabolites in black boxes and amino acids in turquoise boxes) and the genes (italicized) of the enzymes responsible for the reactions based on EcoCyc
                    - emphasis [ref=e751]: E. coli
                    - text: database. Every overexpression (blue circle), downregulation (red circle), and all other miscellaneous modifications including feedback-release (asterisk) attempted in
                    - emphasis [ref=e752]: E. coli
                    - text: for systems metabolic engineering purposes are noted. Convergence and divergence of metabolites are denoted by circular nodes, where some reactions are reversible. As an example for reversible reaction, F6P and GAP converge to form E4P and Xu5P; conversely, E4P and Xu5P converge to form F6P and GAP. Glc, glucose; G6P, glucose 6-phosphate; F6P, fructose 6-phosphate; F1,6BP, fructose 1,6-bisphosphate; GAP, glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate; DHAP, dihydroxyacetone phosphate; 1,3-BPG, 1,3-bisphosphoglycerate; 3-PG, 3-phosphoglycerate; 2-PG, 2-phosphoglycerate; PEP, phosphoenolpyruvate; PYR, pyruvate; Ac-CoA, acetyl-CoA; CIT, citrate; I-CIT, isocitrate; α-KG, α-ketoglutarate; SUCC-CoA, succinyl-CoA; SUCC, succinate; FUM, fumarate; MAL, malate; OAA, oxaloacetate; GOX, glyoxylate; E4P, erythrose 4-phosphate; Xu5P, xylulose 5-phosphate; S7P, sedoheptulose 7-phosphate; R5P, ribose 5-phosphate; Ru5P, ribulose 5-phosphate; RuBP, ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate; PRPP, 5-phosphoribose 1-pyrophosphate; AICAR, 5-amino-1-(5-phosphoribosyl)imidazole-4-carboxamide; His, L-histidine; DAHP, 3-deoxy-arabino-heptulosonate 7-phosphate; DHQ, 3-dehydroquinate; DHS, dehydroshikimate; SHIK, shikimate; CHOR, chorismate; PPHN, prephenate; HPP, 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate; Tyr, L-tyrosine; PHPYR, phenylpyruvate; Phe, L-phenylalanine; ANTH, anthranilate; Trp, L-tryptophan; 3-PH, 3-phosphohydroxypyruvate; P-Ser, 3-phosphoserine; Ser, L-serine; Ac-Ser, acetyl-serine; AcLAC, acetolactate; Val, L-valine; Leu, L-leucine; Ala, L-alanine; D-Ala, D-alanine; Ac-P, acetyl phosphate; AcAc-CoA, acetoacetyl-CoA; Glu, L-glutamate; Gln, L-glutamine; Arg, L-arginine; Pro, L-proline; Asp, L-aspartate; Asn, L-asparagine; AspSA, aspartate-semialdehyde; Lys, L-lysine; HMS, homoserine; Thr, L-threonine; Ile, L-isoleucine; SUCC-HMS, succinylhomoserine; CYST, cystathionine; HMC, homocysteine; Met, L-methionine; Ac-ACP, acetyl-acyl carrier protein (ACP); Mal-CoA, malonyl-CoA; Mal-ACP, malonyl-ACP; AcAc-ACP, acetoacetyl-ACP.

                - generic [ref=e3124]:
                  - heading "Engineering Native E. coli Metabolism" [level=3] [ref=e3125]:
                    - text: Engineering Native
                    - emphasis [ref=e3126]: E. coli
                    - text: Metabolism
                  - paragraph [ref=e3127]:
                    - text: Before engineering
                    - emphasis [ref=e3128]: E. coli
                    - text: as a host organism to produce various chemicals and materials of interest, it is important to engineer and upgrade its native metabolism. Here we present the strategies to engineer the native
                    - emphasis [ref=e3129]: E. coli
                    - text: metabolism that have been designed with tools developed over the evolving field of systems metabolic engineering (
                    - link "Fig. 3" [ref=e3130] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#fig3"
                    - text: and
                    - link "Table 1" [ref=e3131] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#T1"
                    - text: ). These strategies are indeed fundamental for the production of any candidate chemicals and should serve and be treated as the baseline approaches to strain development.
                  - generic [ref=e3132]:
                    - heading "Engineering endogenous biosynthetic pathways for increasing precursor pools" [level=4] [ref=e3133]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3134]:
                      - text: In systems metabolic engineering, the exchange of native promoter with a stronger promoter for increased expression of native gene is a common strategy to increase metabolic flux toward a desired compound. For further improved expression, the genes can also be cloned in a multicopy plasmid. Here, the gene targets are often metabolic genes in central carbon metabolism (
                      - link "27" [ref=e3135] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b27"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "309" [ref=e3136] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b309"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "310" [ref=e3137] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b310"
                      - text: ), biosynthesis of amino acids (

                      - text: ","

                      - text: ) (
                      - link "Fig. 3" [ref=e3162] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig3"
                      - text: and
                      - link "Table 1" [ref=e3163] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#T1"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3164]:
                      - text: Metabolic genes targeted for overexpression depend on metabolic pathways that the products of interest are derived from. The most common target genes for overexpression, however, are the ones from the central carbon metabolism, involving glycolysis, pentose phosphate pathway (PPP), tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, and glyoxylate pathway (
                      - link "Fig. 4" [ref=e3165] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig4"
                      - text: ). Since all of the chemicals produced in systems metabolic engineering are derived from glucose and other renewable carbon sources, the enhancement of the central carbon metabolism, which provides essential key intermediates for all chemicals, is one of the most basic strategies in this field. Still, overexpression strategies of genes in the central carbon metabolism depend on the target product and key intermediates of the product chemicals.
                    - figure [ref=e3166]:
                      - heading "Figure 4." [level=5] [ref=e3167]
                      - paragraph [ref=e3168]:
                        - img "Figure 4" [ref=e3169]

                      - paragraph [ref=e3173]:
                        - strong [ref=e3174]: Examples of metabolic engineering strategies to produce chemicals of interest from central carbon metabolism.
                        - text: "Target products included are (1) D- and L-lactic acid, (2) ethanol, (3) 1,2-propanediol, (4) 1,3-propanediol, (5) butyric acid and 1-butanol, (6) malic acid, (7) fumaric acid, (8) succinic acid, (9) adipic acid, (10) 1,4-butanediol, and (11) itaconic acid. Numbers labeled beside gene names indicate the products that targeted each gene for engineering during engineering. The colors of the numbers indicate modes of engineering: red, downregulation including knockout; blue, upregulation; black, all other miscellaneous modifications including feedback-release, heterologous gene introduction, and mutagenesis for modified enzyme activities. Convergence and divergence of metabolites are denoted by circular nodes, where some reactions are reversible. As an example for reversible reaction, F6P and GAP converge to form E4P and Xu5P; conversely, E4P and Xu5P converge to form F6P and GAP. For abbreviations, see"
                        - link "Fig. 3" [ref=e3175] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: "#fig3"
                        - text: .
                    - paragraph [ref=e3176]:
                      - text: In the TCA cycle, the increased influx of carbons through acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA) alone does not expand the pool of constituent chemicals such as oxaloacetate, malate, and fumarate (
                      - link "Fig. 4" [ref=e3177] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig4"
                      - text: ). Rather, the pool itself is fueled through a couple of direct routes from glycolytic intermediates phosphoenolpyruvate and pyruvate via the reductive branches. The production of chemicals that deplete TCA cycle metabolites thus often requires the refilling of the TCA intermediates. However, increasing TCA cycle flux should be taken with precaution since it can lead to unwanted acetate accumulation due to overflow, offsets the redox balance, and decreases product formation due to increased flux toward biomass. Increase of TCA flux can be achieved by overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3178]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3179] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: (

                      - text: (

                        - /url: "#b310"
                      - text: ) to convert phosphoenolpyruvate to oxaloacetate (
                      - link "Figs. 3" [ref=e3187] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig3"
                      - text: and
                      - link "4" [ref=e3188] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig4"
                      - text: ). In addition to elevating the TCA cycle metabolite levels, overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3189]:

                    - paragraph [ref=e3219]:
                      - text: The pentose phosphate pathway provides valuable precursors for essential chemicals in cells, including aromatic amino acids and nucleotides, in addition to providing reducing powers and energy (
                      - link "Fig. 4" [ref=e3220] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig4"
                      - text: ). Among the various metabolic genes involved in pentose phosphate pathway, the most frequent overexpression targets are
                      - emphasis [ref=e3221]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tktA" [ref=e3222] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11427
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3223]:

                      - text: (

                      - text: ) encoding transketolases, which produces erythrose 4-phosphate, an important precursor of aromatic metabolites, together with xylose 5-phosphate, from fructose 6-phosphate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate. In addition,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3231]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. talA" [ref=e3232] [cursor=pointer]:

                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3233]:

                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11556
                      - text: (
                      - link "323" [ref=e3235] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b323"
                      - text: ) encoding transaldolases were reported to be overexpressed.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3236]:
                      - text: During the production of amino acids and derivatives, desired products can be selectively produced either by enriching the precursor metabolites in central carbon metabolism or increasing the flux after the branch point metabolites (
                      - link "Figs. 3" [ref=e3237] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig3"
                      - text: and
                      - link "5" [ref=e3238] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ). Increasing fluxes toward precursors from central carbon metabolism such as phosphoenolpyruvate and pentose phosphate pathway (
                      - link "20" [ref=e3239] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b20"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "318" [ref=e3240] [cursor=pointer]:

                      - text: ","
                      - link "327" [ref=e3244] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b327"
                      - text: ), and pyruvate (
                      - link "20" [ref=e3245] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b20"
                      - text: ","

                        - /url: "#b319"
                      - text: ","

                        - /url: "#b327"
                      - text: ) can lead to the enhanced production of amino acids and derivatives (
                      - link "Figs. 3" [ref=e3248] [cursor=pointer]:

                    - paragraph [ref=e3274]:
                      - text: Once the carbons from renewable carbon sources are converted to the precursor chemicals in the central carbon metabolism, the fluxes are further diverged into each specific amino acid and its derivatives. Since many of the amino acids share common upstream metabolic pathways, overproduction of a specific amino acid often requires the overexpression of metabolic genes downstream from the branching points (
                      - link "Figs. 3" [ref=e3275] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig3"
                      - text: and
                      - link "5" [ref=e3276] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ). For example, a branched amino acid L-valine is derived from pyruvate in the central carbon metabolism. Park et al. overexpressed
                      - emphasis [ref=e3277]: ilvBN
                      - text: ", which converts 2 molecules of pyruvate into a single acetolactate, with"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3278]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvC" [ref=e3279] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10495
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3280]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvD" [ref=e3281] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10496
                      - text: ", enhancing the carbon flux from pyruvate to α-ketoisovalerate, the branching point of three important pathways producing L-isoleucine, L-valine, and pantothenate ("
                      - link "24" [ref=e3282] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b24"
                      - text: ). In addition, only a single route toward L-valine was reinforced by overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e3283]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvE" [ref=e3284] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10497
                      - text: ", which directly converts α-ketoisovalerate into L-valine, to specifically produce L-valine in the engineered"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3285]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "Fig. 5" [ref=e3286] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "24" [ref=e3287] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b24"
                      - text: ). In another example, another branched amino acid L-isoleucine is derived from a hydroxyl amino acid L-threonine, sharing a biosynthetic pathway from oxaloacetate to L-aspartate to L-threonine. The authors first increased the flux from L-aspartate to L-threonine by overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3288]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. thrA" [ref=e3289] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10998
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3290]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. thrB" [ref=e3291] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10999
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3292]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. thrC" [ref=e3293] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11000
                      - text: genes in a plasmid (
                      - link "Fig. 6" [ref=e3294] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig6"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "21" [ref=e3295] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b21"
                      - text: ). The carbon flux from L-threonine to the target product L-isoleucine was then increased together by overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3296]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvA" [ref=e3297] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10493
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3298]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvH" [ref=e3299] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10499
                      - text: in another plasmid, and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3300]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvC" [ref=e3301] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10495
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3302]: ilvEDA
                      - text: with its promoter exchanged (
                      - link "Fig. 6" [ref=e3303] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig6"
                      - text: ) (

                    - paragraph [ref=e3375]:
                      - text: Despite the overexpression strategies on various target genes, the enhancement of metabolic fluxes toward a desired product is not always successful. A significant fraction of metabolic enzymes are regulated by cellular metabolic states in the transcription, translation, and catalytic activity levels. The use of inducible promoters, including P
                      - emphasis [ref=e3376]: lac
                      - text: ", P"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3377]: tac
                      - text: ", P"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3378]: trc
                      - text: ", or artificial promoters, including J23100, allows successful expression of the target genes. However, the feedback inhibition of the fully expressed enzymes cannot be circumvented in this way. For example, enzymes in L-isoleucine biosynthesis LysC, ThrA, ThrB, IlvA, and IlvIH are feedback-inhibited by the cellular concentration of L-lysine, L-threonine, L-threonine, L-isoleucine, and L-isoleucine, respectively. To overcome the feedback inhibition of the metabolic genes and increase the desired metabolic fluxes toward L-isoleucine, the authors overexpressed genes encoding feedback-resistant enzymes"

                  - generic [ref=e3439]:
                    - heading "Elimination of competing, degradation, and by-product formation pathways" [level=4] [ref=e3440]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3441]: Enhancement of pathway fluxes toward the formation of target product biosynthesis alone is often insufficient to develop a high-performance strain. There exist metabolic branch points draining important precursors or intermediates through by-product formation pathways or degradation pathways. The final product once produced can also be subjected to these draining pathways. Proper blockage of such competitive by-product formation pathways and degradation pathways should be conducted along with metabolic gene overexpression to obtain the synergistic enhancement of the target biosynthetic fluxes.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3442]:
                      - text: In central carbon metabolism, the most common target for pathway deletion is the conversion of acetyl-CoA into acetyl phosphate, which is catalyzed by

                    - paragraph [ref=e3490]:
                      - text: "Gene deletion strategies for flux enhancement in amino acids and derivatives biosynthesis, as in gene overexpression strategies, can be divided twofold: the deletion of genes to enrich the precursors from central carbon metabolism and the deletion of genes after branching points toward various amino acids sharing the same upper pathways. To increase the flux toward erythrose 4-phosphate and thus PPP to extract enough reducing powers,"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3491]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pfkA" [ref=e3492] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10699
                      - text: that competes for the use of fructose 6-phosphate with the initial steps in PPP involving
                      - emphasis [ref=e3493]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tktA" [ref=e3494] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11427
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3495]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tktB" [ref=e3496] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG12100
                      - text: was knocked out (
                      - link "Fig. 5" [ref=e3497] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3498] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). On the other hand, to reduce the drainage of pyruvate, an important precursor for L-valine, L-isoleucine, and L-alanine, toward acetyl-CoA and subsequently toward TCA cycle, fatty acid biosynthesis, and acetic acid,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3499]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. aceF" [ref=e3500] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10025
                      - text: has been knocked out (
                      - link "Fig. 5" [ref=e3501] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3502] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3503]: A combinatorial strategy to enrich precursors in central carbon metabolism and an overexpression of metabolic genes after branching points do increase the flux toward the amino acids of interest. However, it is not enough to specifically overproduce a single amino acid. The fluxes toward other amino acids sharing the same upper pathway increase coincidently, consuming the carbon fluxes for the synthesis of unwanted related amino acids. To prevent such waste, competing pathways from the key branching points are deleted.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3504]:
                      - text: The downstream pathways toward L-valine and L-leucine are divided at α-ketoisovalerate (
                      - link "Fig. 5" [ref=e3505] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ). Deletion of

                      - text: ) converting α-ketoisovalerate to L-valine and

                      - text: (
                      - link "11" [ref=e3511] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b11"
                      - text: ) directing the carbon flux toward L-leucine removed the fluxes toward L-valine and L-leucine, respectively. Chorismate is another branching hot spot for aromatic amino acids biosynthesis. Knockout of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3512]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. trpE" [ref=e3513] [cursor=pointer]:

                      - text: in the long chorismate-to-tryptophan conversion process successfully blocked the waste of carbon fluxes toward L-tryptophan and reinforced the fluxes toward L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine (
                      - link "Fig. 7" [ref=e3518] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig7"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "318" [ref=e3519] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b318"
                      - text: ). The branching point for L-phenylalanine and L-tyrosine is prephenate, and the initial steps toward each amino acid are catalyzed by

                      - text: ). Biosynthesis of L-methionine shares the same biosynthetic pathway with l-threonine and L-isoleucine down to homoserine. Deletion of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3532]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. metA" [ref=e3533] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10581
                      - text: ", which guides the carbon flux from homoserine to L-methionine, successfully redirects the whole carbon flux from homoserine toward L-threonine, L-isoleucine, and derivatives ("
                      - link "11" [ref=e3534] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b11"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "25" [ref=e3535] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3536]:
                      - text: However, the blocking of such branch pathways is powerful enough that essential products for cell proliferation from those deleted pathways cannot be produced in such engineered strains. One of the most traditional solutions to circumvent these auxotrophy problems is supplementing the minimal amount for each of the auxotrophic metabolites or expensive rich components such as yeast extract (
                      - link "10" [ref=e3537] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "11" [ref=e3538] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b11"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "25" [ref=e3539] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "26" [ref=e3540] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "311" [ref=e3541] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "314" [ref=e3542] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b314"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "318" [ref=e3543] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b318"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "330" [ref=e3544] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b330"
                      - text: ). Using the more recent tactic to avoid such problems is knocking down the essential metabolic genes. Na et al. recently applied sRNA for L-tyrosine and cadaverine overproduction, and successfully knocked down two essential genes
                      - emphasis [ref=e3545]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. murE" [ref=e3546] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10621
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3547]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ackA" [ref=e3548] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10027
                      - text: (
                      - link "185" [ref=e3549] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b185"
                      - text: ). Another recent invention, CRISPRi, can also be employed for this purpose. For more information on CRISPRi, refer to the subsection “Repurposed CRISPR/Cas systems” under “Tools for Systems Metabolic Engineering of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3550]: E. coli
                      - text: .”
                    - paragraph [ref=e3551]:
                      - text: In addition to the precursors and intermediates in amino acids and derivatives biosynthesis, the final products themselves are either subjected to degradation or recruited for other product formations. L-Threonine itself is a final amino acid product, but can be further metabolized to produce L-isoleucine. A gene catalyzing the first step from L-threonine toward L-isoleucine,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3552]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ilvA" [ref=e3553] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10493
                      - text: ", was mutated to prevent the loss of L-threonine overproduced ("
                      - link "25" [ref=e3554] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ). To prevent the degradation of L-threonine,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3555]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tdh" [ref=e3556] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10993
                      - text: ", which is responsible for converting L-threonine to an unstable intermediate 2-amino-3-ketobutanoate was removed ("
                      - link "25" [ref=e3557] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: "). Moreover, in the synthesis of L-arginine derivative putrescine and L-lysine derivative cadaverine, Qian et al. eliminated metabolic genes that degrade or utilize these chemicals:"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3558]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. speE" [ref=e3559] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10963
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3560]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. speG" [ref=e3561] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6842
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3562]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. puuP" [ref=e3563] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6643
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3564]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. puuA" [ref=e3565] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6644
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3566]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ygjG" [ref=e3567] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7596
                      - text: (
                      - link "311" [ref=e3568] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "312" [ref=e3569] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b312"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3570]:
                      - text: In the biosynthesis of fatty acids and derivatives, securing the pool of acetyl-CoA, the monomer of fatty acids, is one of the most important factors. In this context,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3571]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pta" [ref=e3572] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG20173
                      - text: encoding phosphate acetyltransferase, an enzyme converting acetyl-CoA into acetyl phosphate, is frequently eliminated for fatty acid and derivative synthesis (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3573] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "16" [ref=e3574] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b16"
                      - text: ). To prevent the degradation and utilization of fatty acids produced,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3575]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. fadD" [ref=e3576] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11530
                      - text: coding for fatty acid acyl-CoA synthetase is commonly deleted (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3577] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "15" [ref=e3578] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b15"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "16" [ref=e3579] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b16"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "17" [ref=e3580] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b17"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "320" [ref=e3581] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ). In addition,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3582]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. fadE" [ref=e3583] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6105
                      - text: (
                      - link "15" [ref=e3584] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b15"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "320" [ref=e3585] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3586]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. arcA" [ref=e3587] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10061
                      - text: (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3588] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3589]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. adhE" [ref=e3590] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10031
                      - text: (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3591] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3592]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. frdA" [ref=e3593] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10330
                      - text: (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3594] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3595]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. yqhD" [ref=e3596] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7564
                      - text: (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3597] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "18" [ref=e3598] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b18"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3599]:
