                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. fucO" [ref=e3600] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10351
                      - text: (
                      - link "12" [ref=e3601] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ), and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3602]: ahr
                      - text: (
                      - link "18" [ref=e3603] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b18"
                      - text: ) have been deleted for free fatty acid and alkane biosynthesis in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3604]: E. coli
                      - text: .
                  - generic [ref=e3605]:
                    - heading "Transporter engineering" [level=4] [ref=e3606]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3607]:
                      - text: Engineering of transporters including exporters and importers is one of the common strategies employed in systems metabolic engineering especially for production of amino acids and related compounds (
                      - link "Table 1" [ref=e3608] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#T1"
                      - text: ). This strategy has been applied in the production of L-valine (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3609] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "23" [ref=e3610] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b23"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "24" [ref=e3611] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b24"
                      - text: ), L-isoleucine (
                      - link "21" [ref=e3612] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b21"
                      - text: ), L-threonine (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3613] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ), putrescine (
                      - link "311" [ref=e3614] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ), and cadaverine (
                      - link "312" [ref=e3615] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b312"
                      - text: ). Specifically, target exporters for overexpression include amino acid transporters
                      - emphasis [ref=e3616]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ygaZ" [ref=e3617] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7405
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3618]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ygaH" [ref=e3619] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7406
                      - text: (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3620] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "23" [ref=e3621] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b23"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "24" [ref=e3622] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b24"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e3623]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. rhtA" [ref=e3624] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG12134
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3625]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. rhtB" [ref=e3626] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11469
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3627]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. rhtC" [ref=e3628] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11468
                      - text: (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3629] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ), and putrescine/ornithine antiporter
                      - emphasis [ref=e3630]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. potE" [ref=e3631] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10753
                      - text: (
                      - link "311" [ref=e3632] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ). Transporters that are involved in uptake of amino acids, on the other hand, must be eliminated for preventing reintroduction of secreted compounds back into the cells. Deletion of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3633]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tdcC" [ref=e3634] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10991
                      - text: for L-threonine production (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3635] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ) and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3636]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. puuP" [ref=e3637] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6643
                      - text: for diamine production fall into this category (
                      - link "311" [ref=e3638] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "312" [ref=e3639] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b312"
                      - text: ). In particular, in the production of L-threonine, deletion of the
                      - emphasis [ref=e3640]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tdcC" [ref=e3641] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10991
                      - text: and overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3642]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. rhtC" [ref=e3643] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11468
                      - text: alone (one of the three exporters) resulted in 15.6% and 50.2% increase in production titer, respectively (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3644] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ). Engineering transporters, however, do not always guarantee an increase in production titer because overexpression of certain transporters has been shown to be detrimental to cell growth. In the production of cadaverine, overexpression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3645]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. cadB" [ref=e3646] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10132
                      - text: retarded cell growth, possibly because of compromise in the membrane integrity (
                      - link "312" [ref=e3647] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b312"
                      - text: ).
                  - generic [ref=e3648]:
                    - heading "Metabolic state-responsive flux balancing" [level=4] [ref=e3649]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3650]:
                      - text: All biological systems continuously interact with environmental changes and adapt accordingly. In the same context, the metabolic state of host microorganisms is dynamic, not only because of its own cellular functions, but also in response to the constant changes in the medium composition, both macroscopic and microscopic. However, the engineered metabolic circuits introduced during metabolic engineering are often driven by strong promoters that are not responsive to the intracellular perturbations. The expression levels of each metabolic gene can be controlled with various tools, including induction systems and libraries of promoters and ribosome binding sites, but it cannot be regulated in response to the dynamically changing metabolic states of the host cells in an automatic or synchronized manner. Consequently, introduction of heterologous genes or frequent manipulation of endogenous genes could yield metabolic imbalances, thus leading to the retardation of cell growth (
                      - link "320" [ref=e3651] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "339" [ref=e3652] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b339"
                      - text: ) or loss of functional genes introduced in the population (
                      - link "339" [ref=e3653] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b339"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "340" [ref=e3654] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b340"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "341" [ref=e3655] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b341"
                      - text: ), decreasing the final product titer. Utilization of the deregulated expression system is intuitive and straightforward for pathway design and construction, but is suboptimal for the production of target products with the best titer.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3656]:
                      - text: To integrate the host metabolic state into the metabolic gene expression and flux control, natural expression-regulatory systems, including two-component regulatory systems (
                      - link "342" [ref=e3657] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b342"
                      - text: ), can be maximally utilized. In 2001, Liao borrowed regulatory components from Ntr regulon in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3658]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "343" [ref=e3659] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b343"
                      - text: ), the function of which is to adjust the host to nitrogen-deficient conditions (
                      - link "344" [ref=e3660] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b344"
                      - text: ). To increase the titer of lycopene in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3661]: E. coli
                      - text: ", Farmer et al. utilized NRI (nitrogen regulator I) coded by"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3662]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. glnG" [ref=e3663] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10385
                      - text: to detect free acetyl phosphate level. By deleting another Ntr regulon component NRII, encoded by
                      - emphasis [ref=e3664]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. glnL" [ref=e3665] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10387
                      - text: ", the authors maximized the capacity of NRI for detecting free acetyl phosphate level and expressed the genes under the control of"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3666]: glnAp2
                      - text: promoter. The introduction of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3667]: glnAp2
                      - text: promoter to the upstream of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3668]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pps" [ref=e3669] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10759
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3670]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3671] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: with NRII eliminated allowed the 50% enhanced production of lycopene and threefold increase in its productivity, compared with a strain possessing the same genetic construct, with the exception that
                      - emphasis [ref=e3672]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pps" [ref=e3673] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10759
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3674]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3675] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: are under the control of P
                      - emphasis [ref=e3676]: tac
                      - text: (
                      - link "343" [ref=e3677] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b343"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3678]:
                      - text: Keasling reported another system that regulates expression of metabolic genes in response to the cellular physiology (
                      - link "320" [ref=e3679] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ). Zhang et al. engineered a natural fatty acid production-related gene expression regulator FadR, of which repressor activity is antagonized by the binding of acyl-CoA (
                      - link "345" [ref=e3680] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b345"
                      - text: ), to stably produce fatty acid ethyl esters (FAEEs). In this report, chimeric promoters P
                      - subscript [ref=e3681]: LR
                      - text: and P
                      - subscript [ref=e3682]: AR
                      - text: were constructed by adding regulatory component or
                      - emphasis [ref=e3683]: fadBA
                      - text: promoter (P
                      - emphasis [ref=e3684]: fadBA
                      - text: ) into phage lambda promoter (P
                      - subscript [ref=e3685]: L
                      - text: ) and phage T7 promoter (P
                      - subscript [ref=e3686]: A1
                      - text: ), respectively. Moreover, P
                      - subscript [ref=e3687]: FL1
                      - text: ", P"
                      - subscript [ref=e3688]: FL2
                      - text: ", and P"
                      - subscript [ref=e3689]: FL3
                      - text: were constructed by further combining P
                      - subscript [ref=e3690]: LR
                      - text: and P
                      - subscript [ref=e3691]: AR
                      - text: with P
                      - emphasis [ref=e3692]: lacUV5
                      - text: . These newly produced three chimeric promoters P
                      - subscript [ref=e3693]: FL1
                      - text: ", P"
                      - subscript [ref=e3694]: FL2
                      - text: ", and P"
                      - subscript [ref=e3695]: FL3
                      - text: enabled different expression of genes in response to the isopropyl-β-D-thiogalactopyranoside and fatty acid concentrations (
                      - link "320" [ref=e3696] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ). By combinatorial adaptation of these promoters to
                      - emphasis [ref=e3697]: pdc
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3698]: adhB
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3699]: atfA
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3700]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. fadD" [ref=e3701] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11530
                      - text: ", a stable, threefold increase in production titer was observed ("
                      - link "320" [ref=e3702] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ). With a large number of biosensors and transcription factors available, strategies for regulating fluxes in response to physiological status are a promising regulatory system to be implemented in many other biosynthetic pathways.
                  - generic [ref=e3703]:
                    - heading "High-throughput engineering" [level=4] [ref=e3704]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3705]: Biological systems are complex, and a huge number of components interact together, forming an immense, intertwined network. Even in a biosynthetic pathway of a single product, at least several to tens of serial catalytic steps are involved, along with competing reactions and regulatory points in the same pathway. Moreover, multiple biosynthetic routes exist to produce a single chemical from glucose or other renewable carbon sources in nature. Therefore, numerous possibilities and strategies have to be tested for designing and constructing an optimal strain, leading to the emergence of systematic and high-throughput approaches.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3706]:
                      - text: There have been many trials to systematically examine huge number of possible combinations and choose the single best strain among them. In 2010, Stephanopoulos reported production of taxadiene, a precursor of an important anticancer drug Taxol, in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3707]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "346" [ref=e3708] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b346"
                      - text: ). Ajikumar et al. designed and constructed a nine-step taxadiene biosynthetic pathway from pyruvate and glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, consisting of an upstream 2-
                      - emphasis [ref=e3709]: C
                      - text: "-methyl-D-erythritol 4-phosphate (MEP) pathway and a downstream module. To maximize the flux, and thus the final titer of taxadiene, the authors selected four enzymatic bottleneck steps consisting of"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3710]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. dxs" [ref=e3711] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6237
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3712]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ispD" [ref=e3713] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7423
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3714]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ispF" [ref=e3715] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11816
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3716]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3717] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: gene products from the upstream module down to isopentenyl pyrophosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl pyrophosphate (DMAPP). Different expression level combinations of these four upstream genes and two downstream genes were tested by using a multivariate-modular approach. The final strain selected showed 15,000-fold increase in the taxadiene titer, with the final concentration of 1.02 g/liter (
                      - link "346" [ref=e3718] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b346"
                      - text: ). Further conversion of taxadiene to taxadien-5α-ol yielded 58 mg/liter, which is 2,400-fold higher than the previously reported taxadien-5α-ol production in yeast, proving the value of a systematic approach (
                      - link "346" [ref=e3719] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b346"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3720]:
                      - text: In addition to modifying promoter strength, ribosome binding sites can be targeted for systematic adjustment of gene expression level. In 2014, Sun et al. utilized libraries of ribosome binding sequences (RBSs) and promoters to systematically optimize the expression level of lycopene production genes (
                      - link "323" [ref=e3721] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b323"
                      - text: ). From a previously engineered strain CAR0001 with
                      - emphasis [ref=e3722]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. dxs" [ref=e3723] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6237
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3724]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3725] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: ", and heterologous"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3726]: crtEXYIB
                      - text: under control of M1-37, M1-46, and M1-93 promoters from a promoter library (
                      - link "347" [ref=e3727] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b347"
                      - text: ), authors further modulated the expression level of central carbon metabolism genes
                      - emphasis [ref=e3728]: sucAB
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3729]: sdhABCD
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3730]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. talB" [ref=e3731] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11556
                      - text: by introducing M1-46 promoter, to adjust cellular ATP and NADPH levels (
                      - link "323" [ref=e3732] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b323"
                      - text: ). The resulting strain showed 76% improvement in lycopene production. The following exchange of RBSs upstream of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3733]: crtE
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3734]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. dxs" [ref=e3735] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G6237
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3736]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3737] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: with RBSL9, RBSL12, and RBSL7 from an RBS library, respectively, further increased the titer by 32%, with the final titer of 3.52 g/liter (
                      - link "323" [ref=e3738] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b323"
                      - text: ). This report demonstrates that further systematic adjustment of RBS strength improves the titer of the target chemicals.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3739]:
                      - text: Systematic repression or knockout of potential targets can also be a powerful approach to improve final titers. However, the traditional knockout strategies are often time consuming when multiple targets are examined in a combinatorial manner. Recently, new technologies to downregulate or knock out multiple targets in a more facile and rapid manner have been developed. One of them is a synthetic regulatory sRNA system. Recently, synthetic regulatory sRNA system was applied for overproducing L-tyrosine and cadaverine by screening the knockdown gene targets (
                      - link "185" [ref=e3740] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b185"
                      - text: ). By reducing the expression of certain genes, the metabolic flux is rebalanced, so the research was aimed at screening the gene target that concentrates the metabolic flux toward the product of interest. First, four intuitive knockdown targets
                      - emphasis [ref=e3741]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tyrR" [ref=e3742] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11042
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3743]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. csrA" [ref=e3744] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11447
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3745]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pgi" [ref=e3746] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10702
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3747]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3748] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: genes and additional 84 target genes were screened. The best strain that produces L-tyrosine up to 21.9 g/liter was made by sRNA-mediated fine-tuned knockdown of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3749]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tyrR" [ref=e3750] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11042
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3751]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. csrA" [ref=e3752] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11447
                      - text: . The fine tuning was achieved by altering the binding energy between the sRNA and the mRNA. Second, for the production of cadaverine, 122 synthetic sRNAs were tested which target individual genes related to cadaverine production or regulatory pathways. Through this procedure, three best strains with
                      - emphasis [ref=e3753]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ackA" [ref=e3754] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10027
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3755]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pdhR" [ref=e3756] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11088
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3757]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. murE" [ref=e3758] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10621
                      - text: individually knocked down, and subsequent fine tuning of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3759]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. murE" [ref=e3760] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10621
                      - text: knockdown level resulted in the best strain with cadaverine titer 12.6 g/liter. It is notable that the gene targets
                      - emphasis [ref=e3761]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ackA" [ref=e3762] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10027
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3763]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pdhR" [ref=e3764] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11088
                      - text: were not the genes involved in the major cadaverine-producing pathway, and that
                      - emphasis [ref=e3765]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. murE" [ref=e3766] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10621
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3767]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ackA" [ref=e3768] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10027
                      - text: were essential genes (
                      - link "185" [ref=e3769] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b185"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "186" [ref=e3770] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b186"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3771]:
                      - text: In addition to the sRNA system, CRISPR-Cas system and CRISPRi together allows more convenient knockout and knockdown target screening. This year, Lv et al. applied CRISPRi system to screen possible knockdown target genes for improving P(3HB-
                      - emphasis [ref=e3772]: co
                      - text: "-4HB) biosynthesis ("
                      - link "348" [ref=e3773] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b348"
                      - text: ). They introduced various sgRNAs targeting multiple genetic loci with dCas9, and successfully controlled 4HB content by regulating the knockdown strengths of TCA cycle genes
                      - emphasis [ref=e3774]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. sucC" [ref=e3775] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10981
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3776]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. sucD" [ref=e3777] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10982
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3778]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. sdhA" [ref=e3779] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10931
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3780]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. sdhB" [ref=e3781] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10932
                      - text: (
                      - link "348" [ref=e3782] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b348"
                      - text: ). In another study, multiplex deletion and insertion of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3783]: E. coli
                      - text: genomic loci using CRISPR/Cas9 system have been demonstrated, and up to three targets were successfully modified (
                      - link "349" [ref=e3784] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b349"
                      - text: ). Contrary to the routine application of CRISPR/Cas-based systems for downregulation studies, CRISPR/Cas9 system has also been employed for upregulation as well (
                      - link "181" [ref=e3785] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b181"
                      - text: ). By the fusion of RNA polymerase ω subunit to dCas9, controlled activation of specific genes can be achieved by simply exchanging sgRNAs or crRNA-tracrRNAs, targeting the upstream of the target genes (
                      - link "181" [ref=e3786] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b181"
                      - text: ). With these systems allowing more convenient modification of multiple genomic loci, systematic approaches to maximize the capacity of a metabolically engineered strain will become more feasible in the near future.
                  - generic [ref=e3787]:
                    - heading "Multiplex-level genome engineering" [level=4] [ref=e3788]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3789]:
                      - text: One of the most powerful ways to improve strains has been random mutagenesis, treating strains with mutagens such as ultraviolet (UV) light (
                      - link "350" [ref=e3790] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b350"
                      - text: ) and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3791]: "N"
                      - text: "-methyl-"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3792]: "N"
                      - text: ′-nitro-
                      - emphasis [ref=e3793]: "N"
                      - text: "-nitroguanidine (NTG) ("
                      - link "351" [ref=e3794] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b351"
                      - text: ) in the presence of proper selection powers. These genome-wide evolutionary approaches allowed tremendous improvement of strains and still propel the strain developments in many industrial fields. In most cases, however, it is difficult to track genetic modifications introduced into the strain, prohibiting proper understanding of the newly developed strains. The seemingly advantageous characteristics introduced during the mutagenesis may impede further enhancements of the strains. In addition, random mutagenesis often leads to retarded growth of the strains and screening for the desired improvement can be laborious. Accordingly, more rational approaches attracted huge attention in academic fields as molecular biology techniques accumulated. Because of the strength of evolutionary strain development, more rational or at least trackable genome-wide evolutionary approaches have been developed and used, including random mutagenesis in preselected, restricted genomic loci and mutagenesis of which consequences are trackable (
                      - link "53" [ref=e3795] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b53"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "191" [ref=e3796] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b191"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "192" [ref=e3797] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b192"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "193" [ref=e3798] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b193"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "197" [ref=e3799] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b197"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "352" [ref=e3800] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b352"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3801]:
                      - text: One of the earliest achievements in multiplex genome engineering was made by using gTME, which elegantly changes the global gene expression pattern by simply mutating a single global transcription machinery (
                      - link "191" [ref=e3802] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b191"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "192" [ref=e3803] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b192"
                      - text: ). By targeting a global cellular transcription machinery σ
                      - superscript [ref=e3804]: "70"
                      - text: for mutagenesis in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3805]: E. coli
                      - text: ", Alper et al. successfully selected and reported various novel strains showing ethanol tolerance, improved lycopene production, and enhanced tolerance for both ethanol and sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS) ("
                      - link "192" [ref=e3806] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b192"
                      - text: ). In the case of lycopene, its production was also improved with the application of MAGE (
                      - link "53" [ref=e3807] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b53"
                      - text: ). During MAGE, simultaneous overexpression and knockout of multiple genes lead to strains with both improved growth rate and lycopene content (
                      - link "53" [ref=e3808] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b53"
                      - text: ). Coselection MAGE (CoS-MAGE), a modified version of MAGE, improved indigo production by targeting 12 operons for promoter exchange with T7 promoters (
                      - link "193" [ref=e3809] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b193"
                      - text: ). TRMR focuses more specifically on the facile tracking of genetic changes in a host population after a multiplex genome engineering procedure (
                      - link "197" [ref=e3810] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b197"
                      - text: ). By detecting barcode sequences inserted together with modification regions using microarray, gene expression level adjustments responsible for tolerance against salicin, D-fucose, methylglyoxal, and L-valine were identified (
                      - link "197" [ref=e3811] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b197"
                      - text: ). In addition, four novel tolerance genes against furfural, a growth inhibitor often found in acid-treated lignocellulosic biomass, were identified with the help of TRMR (
                      - link "352" [ref=e3812] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b352"
                      - text: ). As the above examples indicate, the use of multiplex genome engineering tools not only improves strain performances with the help of evolutionary approaches, but also provides new insights to understand genotypes corresponding to the desired phenotypes.
                  - generic [ref=e3813]:
                    - heading "Omics-assisted approaches" [level=4] [ref=e3814]
                    - paragraph [ref=e3815]:
                      - text: Traditional methodologies for strain improvement include both random and rational approaches (
                      - link "353" [ref=e3816] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b353"
                      - text: ). However, random mutations often accompany undesired alterations of the genome, and rational manipulation of the genome is limited only to a small region of the genome. Thus, the emergence of omics-based approaches was viewed as one of the solutions for these limitations, and a reflection of the increasing need for a holistic and high-throughput approach (
                      - link "37" [ref=e3817] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b37"
                      - text: ). Since the first complete genome sequencing of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3818]: E. coli
                      - text: K-12 strain, a tremendous amount of data on
                      - emphasis [ref=e3819]: E. coli
                      - text: x-omes began to accumulate (
                      - link "5" [ref=e3820] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b5"
                      - text: ). There are many reports on producing valuable chemicals or proteins through omics study, and the notable examples are described in this section.
                    - paragraph [ref=e3821]:
                      - text: A representative application of transcriptome into systems metabolic engineering in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3822]: E. coli
                      - text: is the production of L-valine (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3823] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). Through the transcriptome profile,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3824]: ilvCDE
                      - text: genes, which are part of L-valine biosynthetic pathway, were shown to be overexpressed in the base Val strain. The
                      - emphasis [ref=e3825]: ilvCDE
                      - text: genes were thus overexpressed, resulting in improved L-valine titer from 1.31 g/liter to 3.43 g/liter. Lrp, which positively regulates the level of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3826]: ilvIH
                      - text: ", was also examined. The expression levels of"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3827]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. lrp" [ref=e3828] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10547
                      - text: were shown to have decreased, which was thought to be due to L-leucine fed to the medium for complementing the L-leucine auxotrophy. Thus,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3829]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. lrp" [ref=e3830] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10547
                      - text: was overexpressed in order to offset the negative effect of L-leucine on
                      - emphasis [ref=e3831]: ilvIH
                      - text: expression, showing an increased L-valine titer. Previously unknown valine transporter was investigated by homology searching for the need of transporter engineering. It turned out that the most probable candidate was
                      - emphasis [ref=e3832]: ygaZH
                      - text: . Through transcriptome profile,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3833]: ygaZH
                      - text: was shown to be downregulated, which was thought to be blocking the L-valine excretion. Hence,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3834]: ygaZH
                      - text: was overexpressed, resulting in an even higher L-valine titer. By transcriptome analysis, L-valine titer was increased to a final titer of 7.61 g/liter, about a 5.8-fold increase compared with that of the Val strain (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3835] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). Followed by
                      - emphasis [ref=e3836]: in silico
                      - text: simulation, this strain was developed to produce even more L-valine. Production of L-threonine from
                      - emphasis [ref=e3837]: E. coli
                      - text: "followed a similar approach as described above: following rational engineering, transcriptome analysis, and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3838]: in silico
                      - text: flux response analysis were conducted (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3839] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3840]:
                      - text: Proteomics has also been employed in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3841]: E. coli
                      - text: for producing various valuable products. Examples include antibody fragment production in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3842]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "354" [ref=e3843] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b354"
                      - text: ), determination of a fusion partner for overproducing recombinant proteins in extracellular medium (
                      - link "355" [ref=e3844] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b355"
                      - text: ), and successful production of serine-rich human proteins leptin and interleukin-12 β subunit in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3845]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "30" [ref=e3846] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b30"
                      - text: ). In the particular example of serine-rich protein production, the protein levels of protein elongation factors (including EF-Tu), serine biosynthetic enzymes (GlyA and CysK), and many others were decreased, which was alleviated by overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e3847]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. cysK" [ref=e3848] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10192
                      - text: . Another notable example is the production of spider silk with the help of transcriptomics (
                      - link "29" [ref=e3849] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b29"
                      - text: ). The stress-response proteins were upregulated when spider silk proteins, with high contents of L-glycine, were produced. Along with the fact that L-glycine biosynthetic enzymes GlyA and GlyS were overexpressed, it was hypothesized that the shortage of L-glycine and glycyl-tRNA pool was the main bottleneck in spider silk production. Therefore,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3850]: glyVXY
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3851]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. glyA" [ref=e3852] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10408
                      - text: were overexpressed, successfully increasing the level of glycyl-tRNA and L-glycine, respectively. This led to the successful production of spider silk in a large amount in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3853]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "29" [ref=e3854] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b29"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3855]:
                      - text: Utilizing fluxomics for metabolic engineering is important since concentrating flux to the final product would be an ultimate goal in systems metabolic engineering. Analyzing the whole cell fluxome is mainly done by
                      - superscript [ref=e3856]: "13"
                      - text: C-based flux analysis. Several studies, including fatty acid production (
                      - link "356" [ref=e3857] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b356"
                      - text: ) and L-phenylalanine production (
                      - link "357" [ref=e3858] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b357"
                      - text: ), employed the
                      - superscript [ref=e3859]: "13"
                      - text: C-based flux analysis to examine the flux profile of engineered
                      - emphasis [ref=e3860]: E. coli
                      - text: and suggested further engineering targets. In another study about L-isoleucine production,
                      - superscript [ref=e3861]: "13"
                      - text: C-based flux analysis was conducted and found that intermediates accumulated intracellularly in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3862]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "358" [ref=e3863] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b358"
                      - text: ). Therefore, dihydroxy acid dehydrogenase (DH) and transaminase-B (TA-B) were introduced to redirect the flux toward the product L-isoleucine increasing the titer significantly.
                  - generic [ref=e3864]:
                    - heading "In silico genome-scale metabolic simulation and algorithm-based rational approaches" [level=4] [ref=e3865]:
                      - emphasis [ref=e3866]: In silico
                      - text: genome-scale metabolic simulation and algorithm-based rational approaches
                    - paragraph [ref=e3867]:
                      - text: The metabolic network within
                      - emphasis [ref=e3868]: E. coli
                      - text: is enormous and complex. There have been numerous research and reports on the metabolic pathways and engineering of such pathways in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3869]: E. coli
                      - text: . Nevertheless, it is still almost impossible to intuitively predict the comprehensive or close to near-holistic metabolic profiles of a recombinant
                      - emphasis [ref=e3870]: E. coli
                      - text: and changes in metabolic fluxes once modifications are introduced. With computers and appropriate algorithms representing the metabolic networks and their properties, fair approximations on certain recombinant strains can nonetheless be obtained. Currently, there are plenty of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3871]: in silico
                      - text: tools and resources for analyzing and predicting the metabolic fluxes in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3872]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3873] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "225" [ref=e3874] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b225"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "255" [ref=e3875] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b255"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "256" [ref=e3876] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b256"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "257" [ref=e3877] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b257"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "258" [ref=e3878] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "266" [ref=e3879] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b266"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "268" [ref=e3880] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b268"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "270" [ref=e3881] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b270"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "217" [ref=e3882] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b217"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "272" [ref=e3883] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b272"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "273" [ref=e3884] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b273"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "274" [ref=e3885] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b274"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "275" [ref=e3886] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b275"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "276" [ref=e3887] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b276"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "277" [ref=e3888] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b277"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "278" [ref=e3889] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b278"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "279" [ref=e3890] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b279"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "280" [ref=e3891] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b280"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "281" [ref=e3892] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b281"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3893]:
                      - text: During metabolic engineering procedures, the identification of the appropriate gene knockout targets is an important step. Some of the targets are relatively straightforward once a metabolic network and a target overproduction product are given. However, selection of valuable targets based on intuition is limited for a few initial targets, and unexpected results may arise after a period of time-consuming gene work. Prediction of reliable knockout targets can be delivered with various objective functions and algorithms, including MOMA (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3894] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "258" [ref=e3895] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "338" [ref=e3896] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b338"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "359" [ref=e3897] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b359"
                      - text: ), OptKnock (
                      - link "27" [ref=e3898] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b27"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "360" [ref=e3899] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b360"
                      - text: ), and OptSwap (
                      - link "275" [ref=e3900] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b275"
                      - text: ). Among various amino acids, L-valine was an exemplary study that employed
                      - emphasis [ref=e3901]: in silico
                      - text: gene perturbation analysis to select appropriate knockout targets (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3902] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). To construct L-valine overproducing
                      - emphasis [ref=e3903]: E. coli
                      - text: strain, Park et al. chose engineering targets with intuitive reasoning, followed by a second round of engineering with targets selected based on transcriptomic changes. The resulting strain produced 7.61 g/liter of L-valine (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3904] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). To further increase the L-valine titer,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3905]: in silico
                      - text: gene perturbation analysis adopting MOMA was conducted, using an
                      - emphasis [ref=e3906]: in silico
                      - text: genome-scale metabolic network EcoMBEL979 (
                      - link "266" [ref=e3907] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b266"
                      - text: ). Among the knockout targets proposed by the algorithm were
                      - emphasis [ref=e3908]: aceE/F
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3909]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. lpdA" [ref=e3910] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10543
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3911]: pfkA/B
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3912]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. mdh" [ref=e3913] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10576
                      - text: . Interestingly,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3914]: pfkA/B
                      - text: genes code phosphofructokinase, an enzyme in the initial steps of glycolysis. The genes
                      - emphasis [ref=e3915]: pfkA/B
                      - text: are unlikely selected as knockout targets based on intuitive reasoning, since knockout of them might prune off the glycolytic pathway, impairing the central carbon metabolic pathways that play a central role in energy supply to the host cell. The
                      - emphasis [ref=e3916]: in silico
                      - text: simulation, however, suggested
                      - emphasis [ref=e3917]: pfkA/B
                      - text: since the carbon flux from glucose can circumvent through PPP, eventually reaching the downstream central carbon metabolism. As a result, additional knockout of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3918]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. aceF" [ref=e3919] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10025
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3920]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pfkA" [ref=e3921] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10699
                      - text: (corresponding to 90% of the phosphofructokinase activity in native
                      - emphasis [ref=e3922]: E. coli
                      - text: ), and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3923]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. mdh" [ref=e3924] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10576
                      - text: led to L-valine titer improvement up to 20 g/liter in batch culture (
                      - link "Fig. 5" [ref=e3925] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig5"
                      - text: ) (
                      - link "22" [ref=e3926] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b22"
                      - text: ). Similarly, Yim et al. successfully constructed a 1,4-butanediol (BDO)-producing strain with the help of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3927]: in silico
                      - text: simulations (
                      - link "27" [ref=e3928] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b27"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3929]:
                      - text: Appropriate amplification targets can also be suggested by
                      - emphasis [ref=e3930]: in silico
                      - text: simulations based on genome-scale models. For this purpose, flux response analysis (
                      - link "309" [ref=e3931] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b309"
                      - text: ), FSEOF (
                      - link "258" [ref=e3932] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ), and FVSEOF (
                      - link "276" [ref=e3933] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b276"
                      - text: ) are exemplary algorithms to be employed. Lycopene, an antioxidant, was reported to be produced by a recombinant
                      - emphasis [ref=e3934]: E. coli
                      - text: of which amplification targets were identified by
                      - emphasis [ref=e3935]: in silico
                      - text: simulations. Choi et al. developed FSEOF, an algorithm for gene amplification target selection, and applied it to enhance lycopene production in
                      - emphasis [ref=e3936]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "258" [ref=e3937] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ). They introduced
                      - emphasis [ref=e3938]: crtEBI
                      - text: into an
                      - emphasis [ref=e3939]: E. coli
                      - text: strain for lycopene production, and performed FSEOF on the genome-scale metabolic model EcoMBEL979 (
                      - link "266" [ref=e3940] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b266"
                      - text: ) with information on four additional heterologous reactions using the MetaFluxNet platform (
                      - link "280" [ref=e3941] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b280"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "281" [ref=e3942] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b281"
                      - text: ). The FSEOF simulation suggested 35 target genes involved in central carbon metabolism and 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) pathway (or MEP pathway) among 983 metabolic genes of possible target candidates (
                      - link "258" [ref=e3943] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ). Further verification of the 35 targets by flux variability test narrowed down the candidates into a set of genes responsible for 21 metabolic reactions. Among those 21 genes, Choi et al. examined the overexpression of seven genes,
                      - emphasis [ref=e3944]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pfkA" [ref=e3945] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10699
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3946]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. pgi" [ref=e3947] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10702
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3948]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. fbaA" [ref=e3949] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10282
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3950]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. tpiA" [ref=e3951] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11015
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3952]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. icdA" [ref=e3953] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10489
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e3954]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. mdh" [ref=e3955] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10576
                      - text: ", and"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3956]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3957] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: ", and a combinatorial overexpression of"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3958]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e3959] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e3960]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. mdh" [ref=e3961] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10576
                      - text: ", which showed the best improvement in single-gene overexpression, exhibited 2.7- and 3.2-fold improvements in lycopene concentration and content, respectively ("
                      - link "258" [ref=e3962] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e3963]:
                      - text: "Identification of gene deletion and gene amplification targets are meaningful, but biological systems are not as simple—they are not like binary systems composed of on’s and off’s. Some metabolic steps have linear relationships with the target product production capacity: the stronger the flux, the higher the production capacity; or, the weaker the flux, the higher the production capacity. Many metabolic reactions, however, have a nonlinear relationship to the production capacity: there exists an optimal flux level for the best production capacity. Therefore, to construct the best strain for a target chemical production, the expression level of the major pathways involved should be fine-tuned. Algorithms such as flux response analysis ("
                      - link "23" [ref=e3964] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b23"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "25" [ref=e3965] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "338" [ref=e3966] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b338"
                      - text: ), OptReg (
                      - link "361" [ref=e3967] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b361"
                      - text: ), CosMos (
                      - link "277" [ref=e3968] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b277"
                      - text: ), and k-OptForce (
                      - link "362" [ref=e3969] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b362"
                      - text: ) can help the target gene selection and optimal flux level determination. Production of an amino acid L-threonine was optimized by applying flux response analysis. To produce L-threonine at a high concentration, Lee et al. developed an
                      - emphasis [ref=e3970]: E. coli
                      - text: strain TH07 (pBRThrABC) based on rational metabolic pathway engineering, resulting in a strain producing 10.1 g/liter of L-threonine in flask culture (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3971] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ). To further increase the performance of the strain, Lee et al. performed transcriptome analysis, and obtained
                      - emphasis [ref=e3972]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3973] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: as an engineering target (
                      - link "Fig. 6" [ref=e3974] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig6"
                      - text: ). Both knockout and plasmid-based amplification of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3975]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3976] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: ", however, resulted in the decrease of L-threonine titer, indicating the presence of optimal"
                      - emphasis [ref=e3977]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3978] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: level for L-threonine production (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3979] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ).
                      - emphasis [ref=e3980]: In silico
                      - text: flux response analysis on PPC flux level indicated an optimal flux of 12.2 mmol/g DCW/h with a flux of 4 mmol/g DCW/h in unengineered strain. Exchange of the
                      - emphasis [ref=e3981]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3982] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: promoter with P
                      - emphasis [ref=e3983]: trc
                      - text: allowed higher expression of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3984]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. ppc" [ref=e3985] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10756
                      - text: but lower than plasmid-based amplification in this
                      - emphasis [ref=e3986]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. lacI" [ref=e3987] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10525
                      - text: "-mutant strain, Th19C (pBRThrABC), and the L-threonine titer was improved by 27.7% ("
                      - link "25" [ref=e3988] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ). Similarly, based on transcriptome analysis and flux response analysis, ICL flux was adjusted by
                      - emphasis [ref=e3989]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. iclR" [ref=e3990] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10491
                      - text: deletion, and the resulting strain TH20C (pBRThrABC) showed 51.4% improvement in L-threonine production, compared with the original TH07 (pBRThcABC) strain (
                      - link "25" [ref=e3991] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ). These examples prove the capabilities of
                      - emphasis [ref=e3992]: in silico
                      - text: genome-scale model-based simulations for narrowing down appropriate engineering targets and guiding the path for further engineering. Combined use of these strategies will allow more comprehensive and thorough approaches to develop the best strains producing desired chemicals at high titers.
                - generic [ref=e3993]:
                  - heading "Expansion of E. coli Metabolism with Synthetic Pathways" [level=3] [ref=e3994]:
                    - text: Expansion of
                    - emphasis [ref=e3995]: E. coli
                    - text: Metabolism with Synthetic Pathways
                  - paragraph [ref=e3996]:
                    - text: Many valuable chemicals nonnative to
                    - emphasis [ref=e3997]: E. coli
                    - text: have been attempted for production in
                    - emphasis [ref=e3998]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "Table 1" [ref=e3999] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#T1"
                    - text: ) and the innovative strategies developed and employed to produce these chemicals at high titers (
                    - link "Table 1" [ref=e4000] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#T1"
                    - text: ) are described in this section. Strategies that have been undertaken to expand
                    - emphasis [ref=e4001]: E. coli
                    - text: metabolism with nonnative synthetic pathways should serve as a guide to aspiring endeavors to produce valuable chemicals noninherent in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4002]: E. coli
                    - text: metabolism.
                  - generic [ref=e4003]:
                    - heading "Production of small chemicals noninherent to E. coli" [level=4] [ref=e4004]:
                      - text: Production of small chemicals noninherent to
                      - emphasis [ref=e4005]: E. coli
                    - paragraph [ref=e4006]:
                      - text: Since the initial suggestion of concept (
                      - link "7" [ref=e4007] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b7"
                      - text: ), expansion of
                      - emphasis [ref=e4008]: E. coli
                      - text: metabolism by heterologous expression of proteins for producing desired chemicals enabled production of various noninherent compounds (
                      - link "Table 1" [ref=e4009] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#T1"
                      - text: ). Compounds including ethylene (
                      - link "363" [ref=e4010] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b363"
                      - text: ), monoethylene glycol (
                      - link "364" [ref=e4011] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b364"
                      - text: ), 1,4-butanediol (1,4-BDO) (
                      - link "27" [ref=e4012] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b27"
                      - text: ), 1,2,4-butanetriol (
                      - link "365" [ref=e4013] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b365"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "366" [ref=e4014] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b366"
                      - text: ), ethanol (
                      - link "8" [ref=e4015] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b8"
                      - text: ), higher alcohols (
                      - link "9" [ref=e4016] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b9"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "10" [ref=e4017] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "11" [ref=e4018] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b11"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "12" [ref=e4019] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b12"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "13" [ref=e4020] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b13"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "14" [ref=e4021] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), homoalanine (
                      - link "19" [ref=e4022] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b19"
                      - text: ), adipic acid (
                      - link "324" [ref=e4023] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b324"
                      - text: ), styrene (
                      - link "329" [ref=e4024] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b329"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e4025]: p
                      - text: "-aminobenzoic acid ("
                      - link "328" [ref=e4026] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b328"
                      - text: ), limonene (
                      - link "367" [ref=e4027] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b367"
                      - text: ), 2-butanone (
                      - link "368" [ref=e4028] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b368"
                      - text: ), phenol (
                      - link "319" [ref=e4029] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b319"
                      - text: ), catechol (
                      - link "317" [ref=e4030] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b317"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "326" [ref=e4031] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b326"
                      - text: ), styrene oxide (
                      - link "330" [ref=e4032] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b330"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e4033]: cis
                      - text: ","
                      - emphasis [ref=e4034]: cis
                      - text: "-muconic acid ("
                      - link "369" [ref=e4035] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b369"
                      - text: ), D-glucaric acid (
                      - link "370" [ref=e4036] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b370"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "371" [ref=e4037] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b371"
                      - text: ),
                      - emphasis [ref=e4038]: p
                      - text: "-hydroxybenzoic acid ("
                      - link "318" [ref=e4039] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b318"
                      - text: ), phenyllactic acid (
                      - link "26" [ref=e4040] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ), 4-hydroxyphenyllactic acid (
                      - link "26" [ref=e4041] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ), 2-(4–hydroxyphenyl)ethanol (
                      - link "26" [ref=e4042] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ), phenylacetic acid (
                      - link "26" [ref=e4043] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ), 4-hydroxyphenylacetic acid (
                      - link "26" [ref=e4044] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b26"
                      - text: ), amorphadiene (
                      - link "372" [ref=e4045] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b372"
                      - text: ), alkanes (
                      - link "15" [ref=e4046] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b15"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "16" [ref=e4047] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b16"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "17" [ref=e4048] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b17"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "18" [ref=e4049] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b18"
                      - text: ), FAEEs (
                      - link "320" [ref=e4050] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b320"
                      - text: ), isoprene (
                      - link "373" [ref=e4051] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b373"
                      - text: ), lycopene (
                      - link "258" [ref=e4052] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b258"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "323" [ref=e4053] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b323"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "343" [ref=e4054] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b343"
                      - text: ), polyhydroxyalkanoates (
                      - link "31" [ref=e4055] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b31"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "32" [ref=e4056] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b32"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "33" [ref=e4057] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b33"
                      - text: ), cyanophycin (
                      - link "374" [ref=e4058] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b374"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "375" [ref=e4059] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b375"
