                      - text: ), and various recombinant proteins (
                      - link "29" [ref=e4060] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b29"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "30" [ref=e4061] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b30"
                      - text: ) have been produced, and many of them are not only noninherent in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4062]: E. coli
                      - text: ", but they are also noninherent in any naturally occurring organisms. Production of noninherent molecules generally requires (i) identification of noninherent biochemical reaction(s), (ii) construction of synthetic pathway(s) leading toward the compound(s), and (iii) optimization of the pathway. The noninherent reactions can either be brought in from a different host organism for a known reaction or developed by engineering an enzyme to have nonnatural functions."
                    - paragraph [ref=e4063]:
                      - text: Expression of heterologous gene in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4064]: E. coli
                      - text: allows the extension of metabolic capacity by introducing nonnative reactions and further extension is possible with modification of substrate specificity of the gene product. A notable example is production of wide range of higher alcohols that do not naturally occur in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4065]: E. coli
                      - text: metabolism by introducing heterologous biochemical reaction for expanding the metabolic space. Noninherent alcohols produced using this strategy include 1-pentanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4066] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "14" [ref=e4067] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4068]: S
                      - text: )-2-methyl-1-butanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4069] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 3-methyl-1-butanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4070] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 1-hexanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4071] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "14" [ref=e4072] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4073]: S
                      - text: )-3-methyl-1-pentanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4074] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 4-methyl-1-pentanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4075] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 1-heptanol (
                      - link "14" [ref=e4076] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4077]: S
                      - text: )-4-methyl-1-hexanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4078] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 1-octanol (
                      - link "14" [ref=e4079] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4080]: S
                      - text: )-5-methyl-1-heptanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4081] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), 2-phenylethanol (
                      - link "9" [ref=e4082] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b9"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "14" [ref=e4083] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "331" [ref=e4084] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b331"
                      - text: ), and 3-phenylpropanol (
                      - link "14" [ref=e4085] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ). The main strategy is to use 2-keto acid decarboxylase (KDC) and alcohol dehydrogenase reactions for converting 2-keto acid substrates into corresponding alcohols (
                      - link "9" [ref=e4086] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b9"
                      - text: ). Since certain KDC such as Kivd from
                      - emphasis [ref=e4087]: Lactococcus lactis
                      - text: exhibit broad substrate specificity, it is able to convert various 2-keto acids into corresponding aldehydes by decarboxylation reaction. The aldehydes are subsequently converted to corresponding alcohols since the alcohol dehydrogenase also exhibits broad substrate specificity. The broad substrate specificity can be altered by reaction pocket modification for accepting a broader range of substrates. Specifically, the F381L/V461A mutant of Kivd is able to accommodate larger-size substrates for subsequent conversion (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4088] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ). Furthermore, modification of binding pocket residues in LeuA along with feedback resistance (G462D) allows
                      - emphasis [ref=e4089]: in vivo
                      - text: generation of diverse 2-keto acid variants to be converted by Kivd (
                      - link "14" [ref=e4090] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ). With the feedback-resistant mutant, additional H97A/S139G/N167A LeuA binding pocket mutant allowed microbial production of 4-methyl-1-hexanol and 5-methyl-1-heptanol (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4091] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ), and additional H97A/S139G/N167G/P169A lead to 1-heptanol, 1-octanol, 2-phenylethanol, and 3-phenylpropanol production (
                      - link "14" [ref=e4092] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ). While the enzymes with modified binding pockets are introduced to L-threonine- or L-phenylalanine-producing strains for enhanced precursor availability (
                      - link "10" [ref=e4093] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b10"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "14" [ref=e4094] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b14"
                      - text: ), using strains capable of industrial level production coupled with fed-batch fermentation (
                      - link "25" [ref=e4095] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b25"
                      - text: ) would further improve the noninherent alcohol production.
                  - generic [ref=e4096]:
                    - heading "Alleviation of metabolic burdens and toxicity" [level=4] [ref=e4097]
                    - paragraph [ref=e4098]:
                      - text: Adaptation of heterologous pathways often elicits stress response to the cell because of toxic intermediates or products, or because of the metabolic burden imposed on the cell. Cell growth hindrance is a serious problem, because biomass and chemical production are deeply related with each other. Thus, several breakthrough strategies have been devised and applied for solving these problems. Excessive metabolic burden comes from several factors such as biased codon usage and overexpression of genes and proteins via plasmids (
                      - link "376" [ref=e4099] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b376"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "377" [ref=e4100] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b377"
                      - text: ). In recombinant spider silk production in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4101]: E. coli
                      - text: ", repetitive incorporation of L-glycine imposed a huge metabolic burden on the cell ("
                      - link "378" [ref=e4102] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b378"
                      - text: ). The authors thus increased the L-glycine and glycyl-tRNA pool by overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4103]: glyVXY
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e4104]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. glyA" [ref=e4105] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10408
                      - text: (
                      - link "29" [ref=e4106] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b29"
                      - text: ). Also, production of serine-rich leptin and interleukin-12 β chain was enhanced by overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4107]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. cysK" [ref=e4108] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10192
                      - text: ", alleviating the metabolic burden imposed on the cell ("
                      - link "30" [ref=e4109] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b30"
                      - text: ). By overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4110]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. cysK" [ref=e4111] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10192
                      - text: ", protein biosynthetic capacity was notably enhanced by activation of EF-Tu, and serine biosynthetic pathway was also activated. In this research, proteomic analysis revealed that simply transforming a plasmid can induce stress response to the cell ("
                      - link "30" [ref=e4112] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b30"
                      - text: ). Thus, the plasmid design for gene overexpression is an important factor to be considered. An example in this case was demonstrated in the total synthesis of erythromycin A from
                      - emphasis [ref=e4113]: E. coli
                      - text: ", where reducing the number of plasmids and redesigning them increased the erythromycin A production by 5-fold ("
                      - link "379" [ref=e4114] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b379"
                      - text: ). Toxic intermediates or products can also be detrimental to cell growth and chemical production. In the early days while metabolic engineering was at its infancy, adaptive evolution techniques were used to increase tolerance toward desired chemicals. After the historical construction of the first ethanol-producing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4115]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "8" [ref=e4116] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b8"
                      - text: ), Ingram and colleagues constructed another strain with much higher ethanol tolerance by subculturing the parent strain in media with high ethanol concentration (
                      - link "380" [ref=e4117] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b380"
                      - text: ). Mimicking natural selection can be facilitated in a much more organized way by using systematic approaches. Following the pioneering work using gTME in yeast to enhance ethanol tolerance (
                      - link "191" [ref=e4118] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b191"
                      - text: ), a similar strategy was used in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4119]: E. coli
                      - text: to increase butanol tolerance (
                      - link "381" [ref=e4120] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b381"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e4121]:
                      - text: Although these random approaches were quite effective, limitations in directed evolution and laborious characterization of each mutation have led to development of more systematic and rational approaches. One notable example is the engineering efflux pumps targeting toxic products, especially fuels and pharmaceuticals. Mukhopadhyay and colleagues manifested this idea with biofuel production, where 43 pumps were tested to increase the tolerance along with the production of five biofuels in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4122]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "382" [ref=e4123] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b382"
                      - text: ). The bactericidal effect of plant-derived terpenoids can be overcome by modulating various cellular machineries. Toxicity of geraniol in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4124]: E. coli
                      - text: was successfully alleviated by overexpressing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4125]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. marA" [ref=e4126] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11434
                      - text: ", which subsequently upregulates the expression of AcrAB-TolC efflux pump ("
                      - link "383" [ref=e4127] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b383"
                      - text: ). In contrast, knockout of
                      - emphasis [ref=e4128]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. recA" [ref=e4129] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10823
                      - text: resulted in the extreme sensitivity to geraniol in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4130]: E. coli
                      - text: ", inferring the role of RecA in geraniol tolerance ("
                      - link "384" [ref=e4131] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b384"
                      - text: ). Similarly, acute toxicity of limonene was alleviated by point mutating (L177Q) an alkyl hydroperoxidase AhpC, reducing the generation of toxic limonene-hydroperoxide (
                      - link "385" [ref=e4132] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b385"
                      - text: ). Toxic intermediate leakage is another serious problem. In taxol precursor production, the whole biosynthetic pathway was divided into two modules with varying expression levels in order to minimize the cellular indole level, which inhibits taxol biosynthesis and retards cell growth (
                      - link "346" [ref=e4133] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b346"
                      - text: ). Also, metabolic burden was decreased by reducing the plasmid copy number while maintaining a similar expression level. Synthetic scaffolds can also modulate the metabolic flux to minimize the leakage of toxic intermediate to the cytoplasm. Keasling and colleagues reduced the level of toxic intermediate hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA (HMG-CoA) by bringing the biosynthetic enzymes in close proximity, thus successfully enhancing the mevalonate production (
                      - link "201" [ref=e4134] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b201"
                      - text: ). Bacterial microcompartment can be an alternative strategy since this synthetic compartment can successfully sequester toxic materials within (
                      - link "211" [ref=e4135] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b211"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "212" [ref=e4136] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b212"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "386" [ref=e4137] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b386"
                      - text: ). Alleviation of toxicity can be further enhanced by two-phase cultivation, where an example can be found in phenol production from
                      - emphasis [ref=e4138]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "319" [ref=e4139] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b319"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e4140]:
                      - text: Apart from heterologous pathways and noninherent materials, native chemicals also impose toxicity to the cell when produced in excessive amount. For putrescine and propanol production in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4141]: E. coli
                      - text: ", enhancement of cell growth was successfully achieved by deleting the stress-responsive"
                      - emphasis [ref=e4142]:
                        - link "External, opens in a new tab. rpoS" [ref=e4143] [cursor=pointer]:
                          - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10510
                      - text: encoding RNA polymerase sigma factor (
                      - link "311" [ref=e4144] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b311"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "314" [ref=e4145] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b314"
                      - text: ).
                  - generic [ref=e4146]:
                    - heading "Production of secondary metabolites in E. coli" [level=4] [ref=e4147]:
                      - text: Production of secondary metabolites in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4148]: E. coli
                    - paragraph [ref=e4149]:
                      - text: While the term secondary metabolite cannot be concisely defined, the common characteristics are that they are generally not involved in central metabolism and not required in cell survival. Many secondary metabolites are also in charge of the defense mechanism or the reproduction of the host, and many of them are important pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and health-promoting nutraceuticals, among others (
                      - link "387" [ref=e4150] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b387"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "388" [ref=e4151] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b388"
                      - text: ). Using
                      - emphasis [ref=e4152]: E. coli
                      - text: as a chassis organism is advantageous in that it has a clean genetic background regarding secondary metabolite biosynthesis in which complex feedback regulations do not exist. However, production of secondary metabolites in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4153]: E. coli
                      - text: has been hampered because of high GC contents of native genes, insoluble proteins, noninherent precursors, and lack of modification machinery. The most notable cases—polyketides, terpenoids and alkaloids—are described in this section.
                    - paragraph [ref=e4154]:
                      - text: Polyketides, compounds containing β-keto groups with various degrees of reduction, are classified into three types (
                      - link "389" [ref=e4155] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b389"
                      - text: ). Among these categories, bacterial modular type I polyketide synthases (PKS) are characterized by their multiple modular assembly lines of PKS. Several cases of type I polyketide production in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4156]: E. coli
                      - text: were reported (
                      - link "390" [ref=e4157] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b390"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "391" [ref=e4158] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b391"
                      - text: ) among which the production of erythromycin is the most renowned (
                      - link "392" [ref=e4159] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b392"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "393" [ref=e4160] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b393"
                      - text: ). Production of erythromycin in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4161]: E. coli
                      - text: had been hindered because of the large size of the enzymes (all larger than 300 kDa), posttranslational modification, and the availability of precursors (propionyl-CoA and (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4162]: S
                      - text: )-methylmalonyl-CoA) (
                      - link "394" [ref=e4163] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b394"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "395" [ref=e4164] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b395"
                      - text: ). The first success in producing erythromycin aglycone, 6-deoxyerythronolide B (6-dEB) in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4165]: E. coli
                      - text: was achieved with the productivity of 0.01 mmol g DCW
                      - superscript [ref=e4166]: −1
                      - text: day
                      - superscript [ref=e4167]: −1
                      - text: . The protein solubility problem was solved by lowering the temperature and expressing the enzymes under P
                      - subscript [ref=e4168]: T7
                      - text: . Also, posttranslational modification system and heterologous precursor biosynthetic pathways were introduced (
                      - link "396" [ref=e4169] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b396"
                      - text: ). Following this initial success, many studies focused on overproducing the noninherent precursor, (2
                      - emphasis [ref=e4170]: S
                      - text: )-methylmalonyl-CoA (
                      - link "395" [ref=e4171] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b395"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "397" [ref=e4172] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b397"
                      - text: .
                      - link "398" [ref=e4173] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b398"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "399" [ref=e4174] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b399"
                      - text: ). The highest titer of 6-dEB obtained was 1.1 g/liter, which was comparable to the commercialized host, showing a great potential toward commercialization (
                      - link "400" [ref=e4175] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b400"
                      - text: ). In type II PKS, three crucial enzymes—KS
                      - subscript [ref=e4176]: α
                      - text: ", KS"
                      - subscript [ref=e4177]: β
                      - text: ", and ACP—known as minimal PKS, are iteratively used to synthesize the carbon backbone of their products ("
                      - link "401" [ref=e4178] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b401"
                      - text: ). In contrast to type I polyketides, production of type II polyketides in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4179]: E. coli
                      - text: was rather a disappointment because of the aggregation of the minimal PKS (
                      - link "401" [ref=e4180] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b401"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "402" [ref=e4181] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b402"
                      - text: ). One of the only two minor successes was achieved by expressing fungal PKS instead of insoluble type II minimal PKS for producing SEK26, an anthraquinone (
                      - link "403" [ref=e4182] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b403"
                      - text: ). Another success was reported by overexpressing an alternative sigma factor, σ
                      - superscript [ref=e4183]: "54"
                      - text: ", for the production of oxytetracycline ("
                      - link "404" [ref=e4184] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b404"
                      - text: ). This was possible by increasing the mRNA level of
                      - emphasis [ref=e4185]: oxyB
                      - text: ", encoding KS"
                      - subscript [ref=e4186]: β
                      - text: . However, expressing minimal PKS in soluble form was still unsuccessful. The third family of PKS, also called the chalcone synthase (CHS)-like PKS, has also been problematic in terms of expression in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4187]: E. coli
                      - text: because of factors such as low glycosylation efficiency and pH conditions (
                      - link "405" [ref=e4188] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b405"
                      - text: ). Examples of products from PKSs in this category includes stilbenes (
                      - link "406" [ref=e4189] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b406"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "407" [ref=e4190] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b407"
                      - text: ), flavonoids (
                      - link "408" [ref=e4191] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b408"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "409" [ref=e4192] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b409"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "410" [ref=e4193] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b410"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "411" [ref=e4194] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b411"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "412" [ref=e4195] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b412"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "413" [ref=e4196] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b413"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "414" [ref=e4197] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b414"
                      - text: ), anthocyanins (
                      - link "405" [ref=e4198] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b405"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "415" [ref=e4199] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b415"
                      - text: ), curcuminoids (
                      - link "416" [ref=e4200] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b416"
                      - text: ), and warfarin precursors (
                      - link "327" [ref=e4201] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b327"
                      - text: ). Studies focusing on overproducing precursors, which are much more complex than in type I and II, have also been active (
                      - link "411" [ref=e4202] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b411"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "412" [ref=e4203] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b412"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "416" [ref=e4204] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b416"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e4205]:
                      - text: The second category of secondary metabolites is alkaloids. Not as much progress has been made in producing these compounds in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4206]: E. coli
                      - text: because plant enzymes are not easily amenable to expression in bacterial systems. Thus,
                      - emphasis [ref=e4207]: E. coli
                      - text: was used to produce (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4208]: S
                      - text: )-reticuline, an important intermediate in producing benzylisoquinoline, from L-dopamine and yeast was cocultivated for conversion of (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4209]: S
                      - text: )-reticuline to benzylisoquinoline alkaloids. The subsequent study showed production of (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4210]: S
                      - text: )-reticuline directly from glucose using
                      - emphasis [ref=e4211]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "417" [ref=e4212] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b417"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "418" [ref=e4213] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b418"
                      - text: ).
                    - paragraph [ref=e4214]:
                      - text: Isoprenoids, composed of terpenoids and carotenoids, are an important group of chemicals used for fragrances, fuels, or pharmaceuticals (
                      - link "387" [ref=e4215] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b387"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "419" [ref=e4216] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b419"
                      - text: ). The conversion from the native 1-deoxy-D-xylulose 5-phosphate (DXP) pathway (or MEP pathway) in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4217]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "420" [ref=e4218] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b420"
                      - text: ) into the heterologous mevalonate pathway from
                      - emphasis [ref=e4219]: S. cerevisiae
                      - text: (
                      - link "372" [ref=e4220] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b372"
                      - text: ) was a major breakthrough in this category. Primary studies of terpenoid production started from monoterpenes (
                      - link "421" [ref=e4221] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b421"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "422" [ref=e4222] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b422"
                      - text: ) which has moved on to diterpenes including the acclaimed examples, artemisinic acid (
                      - link "419" [ref=e4223] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b419"
                      - text: ), taxol precursor (
                      - link "346" [ref=e4224] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b346"
                      - text: ), and levopimaradiene (
                      - link "423" [ref=e4225] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b423"
                      - text: ). Of these, taxol and artemisinin precursor production are explained in later sections of the chapter.
                    - paragraph [ref=e4226]:
                      - text: Producing complex secondary metabolites is often assisted with using microbial consortium such as in the production of taxol precursor (
                      - link "424" [ref=e4227] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b424"
                      - text: ) and benzylisoquinoline alkaloid precursor (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4228]: S
                      - text: )-reticuline (
                      - link "417" [ref=e4229] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b417"
                      - text: ). In this strategy, highly intertwined metabolic pathways are distributed to
                      - emphasis [ref=e4230]: E. coli
                      - text: and
                      - emphasis [ref=e4231]: S. cerevisiae
                      - text: ", each taking in charge of the parts that suit the host. Thus, by using this coculture strategy, production of challenging chemicals can be enhanced significantly."
                  - generic [ref=e4232]:
                    - heading "Enhancement of desired biochemical reactions by spatial localization of enzymes" [level=4] [ref=e4233]
                    - paragraph [ref=e4234]:
                      - text: Spatial localization of enzymes in a modular way can be a brilliant solution for heterologous biochemical reactions hindered by side reactions, inefficient distribution of metabolic flux, or unfavorable reaction conditions. One of the notable earlier trials for spatial localization of enzymes is fusing two or more related enzymes together. Several examples demonstrated include the production of galactonolactone (
                      - link "425" [ref=e4235] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b425"
                      - text: ) and glycerol (
                      - link "426" [ref=e4236] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b426"
                      - text: ). Another representative example is engineering type I polyketide synthase (PKS) in which various enzymes are expressed in a fusion polypeptide. This modular system was adopted for producing a single-form alkane and alkenes, pentadecaheptane and pentadecaheptane (
                      - link "427" [ref=e4237] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b427"
                      - text: ), and for producing several long-chain methyl-branched esters in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4238]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "428" [ref=e4239] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b428"
                      - text: ). However, fusing proteins still arouses controversy since the fusion may significantly reduce the original activity of the enzyme. Also, the larger the size of the polypeptide, the harder it gets to be expressed inside the cell. Another feasible engineering strategy for substrate channeling is to couple modular reactions with N- and C-terminal peptide linkers to enhance the interaction of enzymes (
                      - link "38" [ref=e4240] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b38"
                      - text: ). Engineering type I polyketide synthase can give another example in this category (
                      - link "429" [ref=e4241] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b429"
                      - text: ). By engineering N- and C-terminal linkers, epothilone (
                      - link "391" [ref=e4242] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b391"
                      - text: ) and ansamycin precursor (
                      - link "390" [ref=e4243] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b390"
                      - text: ) could be produced successfully. Large-size
                      - emphasis [ref=e4244]: rifA
                      - text: (14.4 kb) and
                      - emphasis [ref=e4245]: epoD
                      - text: (21.8 kb) were divided into two parts, and intermodular linker sequences from 6-deoxyerythronolide B synthase (DEBS) were linked to the C and N termini of the two split enzymes to facilitate the interaction between the two fragments.
                    - paragraph [ref=e4246]:
                      - text: A more efficient system for substrate channeling, synthetic protein scaffold, was devised by Keasling and colleagues (
                      - link "201" [ref=e4247] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b201"
                      - text: ). Synthetic protein scaffolds comprised three types of interaction domains—GBD, SH3, and PDZ—which originated from metazoan cells. This system was applied for overproduction of mevalonate by targeting acetoacetyl-CoA (AtoB), hydroxylmethylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGS), and hydroxylmethylglutaryl-CoA reductase (HMGR) to be used with the scaffold. They were expressed with peptide ligand attached to their C-terminal specific for the corresponding protein-protein interaction domain within the protein scaffold assembly (
                      - link "Fig. 2" [ref=e4248] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#fig2"
                      - text: ). Additional effort of altering the architecture of the scaffold increased the mevalonate titer by 77-fold (around 5 mM), compared with the control strain without scaffold. Glucaric production was also greatly enhanced by using synthetic protein scaffold (
                      - link "371" [ref=e4249] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b371"
                      - text: ). To cope with the rate-limiting
                      - emphasis [ref=e4250]: myo
                      - text: "-inositol oxygenase (MIOX), protein scaffolds were used to enhance the substrate channeling which was successful at increasing the titer about 50% more than previously reported ("
                      - link "371" [ref=e4251] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b371"
                      - text: "). Then, a novel strategy, yet using the similar mechanism to protein scaffold, was developed: DNA scaffold system ("
                      - link "208" [ref=e4252] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b208"
                      - text: ). Onto the custom designed DNA scaffold, target enzymes are bound that are fused with distinct zinc finger domains designed to specifically bind to the scaffold sequence. This system was demonstrated by increasing the titer of resveratrol, 1,2-propanediol, and mevalonate (
                      - link "208" [ref=e4253] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b208"
                      - text: ). Because profound development is being achieved in technologies to design and construct a 2D or 3D structure of DNA molecules (
                      - link "430" [ref=e4254] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b430"
                      - text: ), DNA scaffold is gaining a potential to be developed into 2D or 3D scaffold system, as was demonstrated in the RNA scaffold system (
                      - link "207" [ref=e4255] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b207"
                      - text: ). RNA scaffold is an alternative methodology for organizing intracellular sequential reactions (
                      - link "207" [ref=e4256] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b207"
                      - text: ). The RNA scaffold module has two RNA aptamer domains, PP7 and MS2, which bind to PP7 and MS2 proteins with respective cargo enzymes fused (D0). Extended RNA scaffolds could also be created into one-dimensional (D1) and two-dimensional (D2) assemblies. When applied to hydrogen production using two enzymes, [Fe-Fe]-hydrogenase and ferredoxin (
                      - link "431" [ref=e4257] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b431"
                      - text: ), a significant increase in hydrogen production (11- and 48-fold, respectively) was achieved by adopting D1 and D2 architectures. The RNA scaffold system can be characterized by its organelle-like structured D2 assembly, which had been previously mimicked by BMCs only.
                    - paragraph [ref=e4258]:
                      - text: Whereas active research has been done for engineering these synthetic proteins by various means, the development in engineering BMCs for spatial localization of enzymes was rather slow. Although there are several reports about engineering the characteristics of BMCs (
                      - link "432" [ref=e4259] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b432"
                      - text: ) and heterologous expression of BMCs in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4260]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "433" [ref=e4261] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b433"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "434" [ref=e4262] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b434"
                      - text: ), there is only one report of using this system for biosynthesis of chemicals. After successfully characterizing the signal peptide and fusing this peptide with Pdc (pyruvate decarboxylase) and Adh (alcohol dehydrogenase), ethanol production was enhanced (
                      - link "435" [ref=e4263] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b435"
                      - text: ). Increase in titer was possible because of enzyme localization and regional anaerobic condition made by the compartment that is favorable to ethanol production.
                  - generic [ref=e4264]:
                    - heading "In silico algorithm-assisted synthetic pathway design" [level=4] [ref=e4265]:
                      - emphasis [ref=e4266]: In silico
                      - text: algorithm-assisted synthetic pathway design
                    - paragraph [ref=e4267]:
                      - text: Many of the chemicals noninherent to
                      - emphasis [ref=e4268]: E. coli
                      - text: are naturally produced and observed in other organisms, including other bacterial, archaeal, or eukaryotic species. In such cases, the natural, heterogeneous biosynthetic pathways for the chemicals of interest in other organisms can be artificially introduced into an
                      - emphasis [ref=e4269]: E. coli
                      - text: "host strain. In some cases, however, the heterologous biosynthetic pathways may be unnecessarily circumventing, or the chemicals are indeed found in nature but their biosynthesis may have yet to be elucidated. In more difficult cases, the desired chemicals may not be found in nature. In such situations, novel biosynthetic pathways must be designed. Sometimes the design process is simple: the desired products share most of their structures with inherent metabolites in"
                      - emphasis [ref=e4270]: E. coli
                      - text: and a couple of steps of conversions from such intermediates produces the desired products. In many cases, unfortunately, chemicals of interest are far from inherent metabolites in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4271]: E. coli
                      - text: such that long series of catalytic steps are required, rendering the design of novel pathways difficult. Thus,
                      - emphasis [ref=e4272]: in silico
                      - text: pathway prediction tools are used to present potential novel biosynthetic pathways to researchers.
                    - paragraph [ref=e4273]:
                      - text: One good example of employing an
                      - emphasis [ref=e4274]: in silico
                      - text: pathway prediction tool to find a novel biosynthetic pathway is the production of flavonoid pinocembrin (
                      - link "436" [ref=e4275] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b436"
                      - text: ). Faulon employed RetroPath (
                      - link "294" [ref=e4276] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b294"
                      - text: ) to screen feasible novel pathways producing pinocembrin (
                      - link "436" [ref=e4277] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b436"
                      - text: ). The application of RetroPath suggested 11 novel sets of metabolic reactions, with the best pathway identical to the natural flavonoid biosynthetic pathway. While a combination of various isozymes applicable in the best pathway suggests nine million possibilities, application of RetroPath allowed selecting the 12 best enzyme combinations with the highest scores (
                      - link "436" [ref=e4278] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b436"
                      - text: ). Following construction and examination of the novel biosynthetic pathways in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4279]: E. coli
                      - text: led to a strain producing 1.39 mg/liter pinocembrin (
                      - link "436" [ref=e4280] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b436"
                      - text: ). Additional pathway optimization using ReproPath allowed a 17-fold increase in titer, with a specific value of 24.14 mg/liter (
                      - link "436" [ref=e4281] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b436"
                      - text: ). Similarly, SymPheny Biopathway Predictor allowed the design and construction of a novel 1,4-BDO biosynthetic pathway in
                      - emphasis [ref=e4282]: E. coli
                      - text: (
                      - link "27" [ref=e4283] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b27"
                      - text: ).
                - generic [ref=e4284]:
                  - heading "Process Engineering Aspects" [level=3] [ref=e4285]
                  - paragraph [ref=e4286]: Process engineering is an integral part of systems metabolic engineering. While strain development by systems metabolic engineering is important for increasing production of chemicals in a laboratory setting, it is certainly not enough to bring these microbial systems to industrial standards without optimal process engineering. As such, two strategies—high cell density culture and utilization of various carbon sources—are described in this section to allow these microbial systems to be viable in the production of chemicals in the world market.
                  - generic [ref=e4287]:
                    - heading "High cell density cultivation" [level=4] [ref=e4288]
                    - paragraph [ref=e4289]:
                      - text: High cell density cultivation (HCDC) is an essential part for the microbial production of relevant chemicals on an industrial scale. Fed-batch culture technique is most often used to achieve HCDC in contemporary systems for metabolically engineered microbes. Critical studies for understanding
                      - emphasis [ref=e4290]: E. coli
                      - text: fermentation technology and subsequently increasing cell mass were carried out in 1970s and 1980s in an effort to improve productivity (
                      - link "437" [ref=e4291] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b437"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "438" [ref=e4292] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b438"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "439" [ref=e4293] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b439"
                      - text: ). Growing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4294]: E. coli
                      - text: to achieve density as high as 100 g/liter cell mass in liquid medium usually refers to this method of cultivation, and certain cases for producing various compounds and proteins requires this cultivation technique (
                      - link "438" [ref=e4295] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b438"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "440" [ref=e4296] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b440"
                      - text: ). Production of proteins including growth hormones (
                      - link "441" [ref=e4297] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b441"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "442" [ref=e4298] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b442"
                      - text: ), interleukins (
                      - link "30" [ref=e4299] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b30"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "443" [ref=e4300] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b443"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "444" [ref=e4301] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b444"
                      - text: ), and compounds including poly(3-hydroxybutyric acid) (
                      - link "445" [ref=e4302] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b445"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "446" [ref=e4303] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b446"
                      - text: ) are some of the notable examples that employed HCDC for high production titers. The feeding mechanisms include exponential feeding, constant feeding, increased feeding, pH stat, dissolved oxygen (DO) stat, and substrate concentration control (
                      - link "438" [ref=e4304] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b438"
                      - text: ). The widely accepted biggest problem in HCDC process performance is the accumulation of acetate that inhibits growth and prevents recombinant protein product formation (
                      - link "438" [ref=e4305] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b438"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "440" [ref=e4306] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b440"
                      - text: ). While glycerol prevents acetate formation, possibly because of the relatively slower intake compared with that of glucose (
                      - link "447" [ref=e4307] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b447"
                      - text: ), glycerol is generally more expensive than glucose (
                      - link "448" [ref=e4308] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b448"
                      - text: ) and a slower growth rate is observed (
                      - link "447" [ref=e4309] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b447"
                      - text: ). Although crude glycerol is abundantly produced in the biodiesel industry as a by-product, impurities make it less attractive as a universal carbon source (
                      - link "449" [ref=e4310] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b449"
                      - text: ). However, acetate formation can be greatly reduced when growth rate is slowed down (
                      - link "438" [ref=e4311] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b438"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "440" [ref=e4312] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b440"
                      - text: ). In a study where exponential feeding fed-batch cultivation was combined with pH stat, the problem with acetate accumulation was solved by reducing the specific growth rate (
                      - emphasis [ref=e4313]: μ
                      - text: = 0.093 h
                      - superscript [ref=e4314]: −1
                      - text: ) and 101 g/liter cell biomass was also achieved (
                      - link "450" [ref=e4315] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b450"
                      - text: ). Although the drawback was carbon flux going mostly toward biomass formation instead of product formation, this study presents a potential strategy for reducing acetate formation for future applications.
                  - generic [ref=e4316]:
                    - heading "Utilization of various carbon sources" [level=4] [ref=e4317]
                    - paragraph [ref=e4318]:
                      - text: One of the ultimate goals envisioned in industrial bioprocesses is to use renewable nonfood biomass for the production of desired chemicals. It is therefore of utmost importance for microbes to be able to utilize not only glucose, but also a large portfolio of carbon sources. There have been several successful efforts to engineer
                      - emphasis [ref=e4319]: E. coli
                      - text: such that it can utilize carbon sources including glycerol (
                      - link "451" [ref=e4320] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b451"
                      - text: ), xylose (
                      - link "365" [ref=e4321] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b365"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "452" [ref=e4322] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b452"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "453" [ref=e4323] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b453"
                      - text: ), sucrose (
                      - link "454" [ref=e4324] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b454"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "455" [ref=e4325] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b455"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "456" [ref=e4326] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b456"
                      - text: ), cellobiose (
                      - link "453" [ref=e4327] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b453"
                      - text: ), xylan (
                      - link "457" [ref=e4328] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b457"
                      - text: ), and cellulose (
                      - link "457" [ref=e4329] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b457"
                      - text: ). One notable example is the development of sucrose-utilizing
                      - emphasis [ref=e4330]: E. coli
                      - text: K-12 strain to produce L-threonine while maintaining its production integrity (
                      - link "455" [ref=e4331] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b455"
                      - text: ). In this example, sucrose-utilizing operons were introduced to the host, where sucrose was observed to be hydrolyzed into glucose and fructose in the extracellular space and subsequently transported into the cell by the respective uptake systems (
                      - link "455" [ref=e4332] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b455"
                      - text: ). This study is a huge leap in strain development because a limited number of
                      - emphasis [ref=e4333]: E. coli
                      - text: strains such as
                      - emphasis [ref=e4334]: E. coli
                      - text: W (
                      - link "458" [ref=e4335] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b458"
                      - text: ) and
                      - emphasis [ref=e4336]: E. coli
                      - text: EC3132 (
                      - link "459" [ref=e4337] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b459"
                      - text: ) have been characterized to utilize sucrose despite the depth of accumulated knowledge for many of the well-studied model strains including K-12, B, and C (
                      - link "455" [ref=e4338] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b455"
                      - text: ","
                      - link "456" [ref=e4339] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b456"
                      - text: ). Another notable example describes the consolidation of cellulolytic enzyme expression, pretreated biomass hydrolysis, and production of biofuels from cellulosic biomass (
                      - link "457" [ref=e4340] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: "#b457"
                      - text: ). Implementing cellulolytic components including cellulase and β-glucosidase allowed the utilization of cellulose, while xylobiosidase and endoxylanase allowed the utilization of xylan. With the use of this system,
                      - emphasis [ref=e4341]: E. coli
                      - text: was able to grow on ionic liquid-treated switchgrass,
                      - emphasis [ref=e4342]: Eucalyptus globulus
                      - text: and yard waste to produce value-added fuels. While the product titers (28 mg/liter butanol, 1.7 mg/liter pinene, and 71 mg/liter FAEEs) are low for industrial applications, this study demonstrates important strides toward utilizing pretreated biomass for renewable chemical production.
              - generic [ref=e4343]:
                - 'heading "INDUSTRIAL LEVEL PRODUCTION OF CHEMICALS BY SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF E. COLI : CASE STUDIES" [level=2] [ref=e4344]':
                  - text: INDUSTRIAL LEVEL PRODUCTION OF CHEMICALS BY SYSTEMS METABOLIC ENGINEERING OF
                  - emphasis [ref=e4345]: E. COLI
                  - text: ": CASE STUDIES"
                - paragraph [ref=e4346]:
                  - text: With the use of the strategies of systems metabolic engineering, an increasing number of engineered
                  - emphasis [ref=e4347]: E. coli
                  - text: strains are being developed for the production of diverse chemicals and materials. In this section, we present the two examples acclaimed in this field of metabolic engineering, where the microbial production of these chemicals demonstrates the sheer capacity of what can be envisioned and achieved with systems metabolic engineering. The success of 1,4-butanediol and artemisinin certainly showcases what systems metabolic engineering can deliver to the sustainable chemical industry.
                - generic [ref=e4348]:
                  - heading "1,4-BDO" [level=3] [ref=e4349]
                  - paragraph [ref=e4350]:
                    - text: The most notable example for developing a microorganism to produce chemicals and successful transition to industrial scale is 1,4-BDO production in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4351]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "27" [ref=e4352] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b27"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "460" [ref=e4353] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b460"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "461" [ref=e4354] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b461"
                    - text: ). 1,4-BDO is an industrially important compound for butadiene, tetrahydrofuran, polytetrahydrofuran, polybutylene terephthalate, polyurethane, and other polyester applications. The petrochemical world market production for 1,4-BDO has reached 1.3 million tons per year (
                    - link "462" [ref=e4355] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b462"
                    - text: ). A metabolic pathway prediction tool SymPheny was used to design a novel pathway leading to 1,4-BDO from
                    - emphasis [ref=e4356]: E. coli
                    - text: central metabolism. The novel pathway consists of
                    - emphasis [ref=e4357]: E. coli sucCD
                    - text: ","
                    - emphasis [ref=e4358]: adh
                    - text: ", and"
                    - emphasis [ref=e4359]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. sucA" [ref=e4360] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10979
                    - text: ","
                    - emphasis [ref=e4361]:
                      - text: Porphyromonas gingivalis
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. sucD" [ref=e4362] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10982
                    - text: and
                    - emphasis [ref=e4363]: 4hdb
                    - text: ", and codon-optimized version of"
                    - emphasis [ref=e4364]:
                      - text: Clostridium beijerinckii
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. ald" [ref=e4365] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10035
                    - text: . To improve flux toward TCA cycle, R163L mutation was also introduced to citrate synthase encoded by
                    - emphasis [ref=e4366]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. gltA" [ref=e4367] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10402
                    - text: . The strain was further optimized by OptKnock simulation identifying deletion candidates (
                    - link "463" [ref=e4368] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b463"
                    - text: ). Accordingly, endogenous
                    - emphasis [ref=e4369]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. adhE" [ref=e4370] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10031
                    - text: ","
                    - emphasis [ref=e4371]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. pflB" [ref=e4372] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10701
                    - text: ","
                    - emphasis [ref=e4373]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. ldh" [ref=e4374] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10231
                    - text: ","
                    - emphasis [ref=e4375]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. mdh" [ref=e4376] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10576
                    - text: ", and"
                    - emphasis [ref=e4377]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. arcA" [ref=e4378] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10061
                    - text: deletions were carried out. Endogenous
                    - emphasis [ref=e4379]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. lpdA" [ref=e4380] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10543
                    - text: was also replaced with
                    - emphasis [ref=e4381]:
                      - text: Klebsiella pneumonia
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. lpdA" [ref=e4382] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10543
                    - text: for improved anaerobic activity. While this demonstrated the highest reported 1,4-BDO with 18 g/liter in 5 days of fermentation in 2 liter-scale (
                    - link "27" [ref=e4383] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b27"
                    - text: ), the strain was continuously optimized and an accumulation of more than 50 genetic changes was made to the final production strain (
                    - link "461" [ref=e4384] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b461"
                    - text: ). From the study, most of the carbon flux has been determined to be directed toward 1,4-BDO by radiolabeled
                    - superscript [ref=e4385]: "13"
                    - text: C-based flux analysis, suggesting that there are little by-products to be eliminated for downstream processes. Moreover, the oxygen uptake rate was also optimized to reduce cell biomass formation since additional cost is required to remove biomass at the downstream processes. It is important to optimize oxygen uptake rate as it determines carbon propagation toward cell biomass formation—a reduced respiration signifies a fewer number of cells producing the target chemical, which in turn requires more cultivation time.
                  - paragraph [ref=e4386]:
                    - text: Successful optimization of strain performance and process engineering has led to the production titer of 120 g/liter with 3 g/liter/h productivity which are feasible values for industrial applications (
                    - link "461" [ref=e4387] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b461"
                    - text: ). This technology has been recently licensed to BASF for industrial scale-up process and further development. BASF additionally possesses the capability to purify 1,4-BDO using a three-stage fractional distillation (
                    - link "464" [ref=e4388] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b464"
                    - text: ), and the production of butadiene and polytetrahydrofuran for spandex applications with this renewable 1,4-BDO produced is also under development.
                - generic [ref=e4389]:
                  - heading "Artemisinic Acid" [level=3] [ref=e4390]
                  - paragraph [ref=e4391]:
                    - text: Artemisinin is a potent antimalarial drug extracted from plant
                    - emphasis [ref=e4392]: Artemisia annua
                    - text: (
                    - link "465" [ref=e4393] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b465"
                    - text: ). While artemisinic acid production in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4394]: S. cerevisiae
                    - text: was a brilliant success in order to adjust the production cost to be sold in the developing world (
                    - link "466" [ref=e4395] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b466"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "467" [ref=e4396] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b467"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "468" [ref=e4397] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b468"
                    - text: ), it would not have been possible without the initial development of artemisinic acid biosynthetic pathways and precursors in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4398]: E. coli
                    - text: (
                    - link "372" [ref=e4399] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b372"
                    - text: ). Biosynthesis of artemisinic acid was put forward by the first success of amorpha-4,11-diene production achieved by introducing the mevalonate pathway from
                    - emphasis [ref=e4400]: S. cerevisiae
                    - text: in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4401]: E. coli
                    - text: to produce IPP and DMAPP, the building blocks for isoprenoid production (
                    - link "372" [ref=e4402] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b372"
                    - text: "). In this pioneering study, the heterologous mevalonate pathway was distributed into two operons: upstream ("
                    - emphasis [ref=e4403]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. atoB" [ref=e4404] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG11672
                      - text: ", HMGS, tHMGR"
                    - text: ) and downstream (
                    - emphasis [ref=e4405]:
                      - text: ERG12, ERG8, MVD1,
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. idi" [ref=e4406] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=G7508
                    - text: ", and"
                    - emphasis [ref=e4407]:
                      - link "External, opens in a new tab. ispA" [ref=e4408] [cursor=pointer]:
                        - /url: http://biocyc.org/ECOLI/NEW-IMAGE?type=GENE&object=EG10508
                    - text: ). Codon optimization of
                    - emphasis [ref=e4409]: ADS
                    - text: (amorphadiene synthase) and addition of glycerol in the medium enabled the production of amorphadiene up to 24 μg caryophyllene equivalents/ml. Following this initial success, many trials were done to increase the production of terpenes by optimizing the mevalonate pathway (
                    - link "469" [ref=e4410] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b469"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "470" [ref=e4411] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b470"
                    - text: ","
                    - link "471" [ref=e4412] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b471"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e4413]:
                    - text: In addition to these metabolic engineering strategies, endeavors undertaken to maximize the mevalonate production includes the utilization of synthetic protein scaffold to modulate the metabolic flux (
                    - link "201" [ref=e4414] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b201"
                    - text: ), and engineering the tunable intergenic regions (TIGRs) to regulate the expression of genes inside an operon (
                    - link "182" [ref=e4415] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b182"
                    - text: ). However, at this point, Keasling and colleagues speculated that the production of artemisinin in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4416]: E. coli
                    - text: had been underestimated because of the volatility of amorphadiene in water. Therefore, they set up a two-phase partitioning bioreactor using a dodecane organic phase, successfully preventing the evaporation of amorphadiene (
                    - link "472" [ref=e4417] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b472"
                    - text: ). In 2009, by using alternative mevalonate biosynthetic enzymes and optimization of fermentation process in regard to glucose and nitrogen restriction, amorphadiene titer had significantly escalated to as high as 29.7 g/liter (
                    - link "473" [ref=e4418] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b473"
                    - text: ).
                  - paragraph [ref=e4419]:
                    - text: Obtaining such high titer was a remarkable success, and commercialization was expected to be at hand; however, chemical conversion from amorphadiene to artemisinic acid was tough, and only a minor success was achieved for this conversion
                    - emphasis [ref=e4420]: in vivo
                    - text: . Keasling and colleagues successfully expressed plant P450s in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4421]: E. coli
                    - text: heterologously and directly produced artemisinic acid at titers of >100 mg/liter with the
                    - emphasis [ref=e4422]: E. coli
                    - text: DH1 strain, engineering amorphadiene oxidase (AMO) and using appropriate P450 reductase (CPR) from
                    - emphasis [ref=e4423]: A. annua
                    - text: as a redox partner (
                    - link "474" [ref=e4424] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b474"
                    - text: ). Despite much higher production of amorphadiene in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4425]: E. coli
                    - text: than in
                    - emphasis [ref=e4426]: S. cerevisiae
                    - text: ", the inability of"
                    - emphasis [ref=e4427]: E. coli
                    - text: to express P450 enzymes efficiently and its low conversion rate from amorphadiene to artemisinic acid has led to change of the chassis organism to yeast (
                    - link "475" [ref=e4428] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b475"
                    - text: ). Following the shift in host organism, a revolutionary step-up toward commercialization was achieved in yeast where 25 g/liter of artemisinic acid was produced followed by chemical conversion to artemisinin with 40 to 45% of overall yield (
                    - link "475" [ref=e4429] [cursor=pointer]:
                      - /url: "#b475"
                    - text: ).
              - generic [ref=e4430]:
                - heading "CONCLUSIONS" [level=2] [ref=e4431]: CONCLUSIONS
                - paragraph [ref=e4432]:
                  - text: With the advent of systems metabolic engineering,
                  - emphasis [ref=e4433]: E. coli
                  - text: has been thoroughly exploited for the production of useful chemicals and materials far beyond its native capabilities. Systems metabolic engineering not only adopts tools extensively from various disciplines, but also uses emerging tools tailored to meet the specific needs for strain improvement. Complementing the exhaustive depository of tools readily available, innovative strategies for systems metabolic engineering of
                  - emphasis [ref=e4434]: E. coli
                  - text: have since also been demonstrated to produce chemicals in pioneering approaches. Taken together, several of the chemicals produced by these engineered strains have met industrial production standards, already contributing a substantial supply to the world market. It must be noted that many of the chemical products attempted for production in
                  - emphasis [ref=e4435]: E. coli
                  - text: admittedly serve only as proofs-of-concept, and further engineering efforts are therefore required to manifest significance viable in industrial production standards.
                - paragraph [ref=e4436]:
                  - text: Engineered microbes such as
                  - emphasis [ref=e4437]: E. coli
                  - text: have the potential to dominate the production of chemicals—from petroleum derivatives to pharmaceuticals. Driven by the influx of new tools and strategies, the capacity with which systems metabolic engineering of microbes holds for the future is certainly limitless. While systems metabolic engineering is no longer in its infancy, it is now positioned to embrace the next generation of interdisciplinary principles and innovation. This new era of biotechnology, in its consummate maturity, promises the sustainable production of useful chemicals and materials from renewable resources.
